## build-mismatch-turns-unattended-mounts-into-displacing.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading. In `crates/farhelm-ui/assets/terminal.js` one boolean means both "an unattended
  attach is allowed" and "this attach does not displace anyone". Once a build mismatch makes unattended attachment
  manual-only, that boolean is false, so a tab newly discovered by a successful detail refresh mounts on the ordinary,
  displacing route. The supervisor then takes the session's terminal away from whoever is attached in another window,
  without anyone asking for a takeover. SPEC.md's takeover rules (unattended recovery never displaces, and "One GUI at a
  time" explicitly keeps them) say this must not happen.
- Decision: the user asked on 2026-10-11 for findings whose outcome is straightforward and needs no significant
  complexity or redesign to be triaged without discussion. Precedent: `takeover-latch-misses-attaching-tabs.md` and
  `new-tab-mount-displaces-owner-during-recovery.md` were both fixed under the same rule.
- Completion criteria: an attach that is not an explicit takeover never takes the displacing route, whatever the build
  mismatch state; under a mismatch, a newly discovered tab either mounts on the non-displacing route or waits for the
  user's explicit action. Keep forbidden unattended mounts and intentional takeover as separate states. Add a regression
  test if it fits the existing terminal-tab browser specs. Stop and bring it back to the user if this needs more than a
  contained change to the mount decision. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete; jj change `lzvmtmzv`, bookmark `plan/ui-layout-and-escaping-fixes/01-ui-fixes`;
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/1932/changes.

## seen-state-queue-acknowledge-newer-choice-sending-it.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading. The read/unread write queue in `crates/farhelm-ui/src/api.rs` decides there is
  nothing newer to send by comparing values. When this window's mark-read is still waiting for its reply, another window
  marks the session unread, and this window marks it read again, the new choice equals the one in flight, so the queue
  finishes without sending it and reports success while the stored state stays unread. The preference queue beside it
  handles exactly this case with a flag recording that a choice arrived after the send.
- Decision: the user asked on 2026-10-11 for findings whose outcome is straightforward and needs no significant
  complexity or redesign to be triaged without discussion. SPEC.md "One GUI at a time" says to fix concurrent-GUI races
  when the fix is easy and adds little complexity, and the existing preference-queue pattern makes it easy.
- Completion criteria: a choice recorded after a write was sent is always sent before the queue reports completion, even
  when it equals the value in flight, using the same mechanism as the preference queue. Add a unit test for the
  equal-valued case. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete; jj change `lzvmtmzv`, bookmark `plan/ui-layout-and-escaping-fixes/01-ui-fixes`;
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/1932/changes.

## uninstall-race-first-time-service-setup.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading, not reproduced. When no service unit directory exists yet, uninstall takes no setup
  lock (`crates/farhelm/src/setup.rs`, the optional unit-directory lock), so a first-ever `farhelm helm setup` running
  at the same time can create the directory and publish service definitions after uninstall's last check. Uninstall then
  removes the executable and reports success, leaving services that point at a deleted program. Linux flat installations
  only, and only when the two commands genuinely overlap. SPEC.md "Concurrent and interrupted runs" requires overlapping
  setup and uninstall to end in a correct state and does not carve out this case.
- Decision: the user asked on 2026-10-11 for findings whose outcome is straightforward and needs no significant
  complexity or redesign to be triaged without discussion. Precedent: `installer-stale-lock-recovery-not-exclusive.md`
  was fixed under the same spec rule.
- Completion criteria: setup and uninstall exclude each other even when the unit directory does not exist yet, or the
  conflicting transition is refused by an equivalent guard, so an overlapping run can no longer leave service
  definitions pointing at a removed executable while uninstall reports success. Add a focused test if one fits the
  existing setup/uninstall tests without new machinery. Stop and bring it back to the user if this needs a redesign of
  the lock layout. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `pending`, waiting on the user: locking only when uninstall can reach the user manager leaves a first-setup
  race when another invocation can reach it. Locking the fallback unit directory also misses different manager and
  caller directories; inspecting the installer lock without acquiring it still races its creation. One option is to
  refuse standalone uninstall whenever the manager cannot identify its unit directory, losing the existing CLI-only
  no-manager removal path. The behavior-preserving option is a separate shared-exclusion change: reuse the installer
  lock for precisely the installations eligible for flat removal, or authorize an executable-keyed lock that does not
  require writing beside the binary. That needs an explicit participation contract for supported executable paths and
  installation transitions. Recommend that separately scoped exclusion change. No partial fix shipped; the original
  setup/uninstall race remains unfixed. Feedback file and index entry retained.
- Superseded 2026-10-19: re-checked on main a7165396 by code reading. Linux flat uninstall needs the
  `.farhelm-installation` record, which only older installers wrote: current `scripts/install.sh` refuses Linux and
  removes that record as the previous layout's, and nothing current creates one. The race then also needs the two
  commands to overlap. That matches `review_feedback_queue/FILTER.md`, "Upgrades from older releases combined with
  another rare condition" (added 2026-10-14, after the decision above); none of its exceptions applies.
- Outcome (2026-10-19, supersedes the above): `other`.
- Decision (2026-10-19): on the cross-cutting triage page, the user accepted "remove as filtered" for this item.
- Completion criteria: remove the feedback file and its index entry; no spec or code change.
- Execution: complete (queue cleanup during triage, per `review_feedback_queue/AGENTS.md`, "Lifecycle").

## failed-sink-record-hides-older-reaper.md

- Outcome: `other`.
- Assessment: mechanism confirmed by reading, reachability not verified. When a failed output-client record replaces one
  whose older reaper is still running (in practice one stuck retrying), that reaper is no longer tracked, so a planned
  stop's wait counts as settled, the supervisor exits with the client still open, and the expiry quiet-down does not
  run. The worst case is the known tmux abort on abrupt closure of an output-bearing client.
- Decision: skipped under the triage rule for findings covered by the specifications. SPEC_impl.md (the output-client
  teardown paragraph) says further defenses against that tmux abort are not worth significant complexity without an
  observed abort on tmux 3.7c or later, and that "a rare path bypassing the existing safe-teardown discipline is not a
  reason for further design or code". The `shutdown-expiry.md` decision applied that principle to planned stops, and
  `sink-shutdown-retries-forever-after-delete.md` accepted this unregistered-reaper gap on 2026-10-01. Because the
  consequence could be highest-bucket, an independent fresh-context reviewer checked the drop against that text on
  2026-10-11 and agreed.
- Completion criteria: remove the feedback file and its index entry immediately, without code or spec changes.
- Execution: `complete`; removed the feedback file and index entry during triage.

## startup-verification-skipped-no-stale-client-initially.md

- Outcome: `other`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading. Startup recovery skips its steadiness check when the first client listing is empty,
  so a predecessor's output client that attaches a moment later is never seen. That needs the previous supervisor to
  have died mid-spawn without running any cleanup code, and the supervisor to restart before the orphaned client
  finishes attaching. The late client's owner is dead, so it either closes abruptly (the tmux abort) or stays until the
  next start's sweep; panes stay readable through the new supervisor's own sink.
- Decision: skipped under the triage rule for findings covered by the specifications. BUGS.md accepts the abrupt-death
  case ("only a death that runs no code is left here"), and SPEC_impl.md's output-client teardown paragraph says a rare
  path bypassing the safe-teardown discipline is not a reason for further design or code without an observed abort on
  tmux 3.7c or later. Because the consequence could be highest-bucket, an independent fresh-context reviewer checked the
  drop on 2026-10-11 and agreed.
- Completion criteria: remove the feedback file and its index entry immediately, without code or spec changes.
- Execution: `complete`; removed the feedback file and index entry during triage.

## classification-counts-runner-failures-deterministic-test-failures.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed. `classify()` in `deflake/bin/deflake` judges each per-test rerun only by the recorder's exit
  status, so three reruns that fail for runner reasons (a build error, a recorder refusal) produce a "deterministic"
  verdict and can send the agent after a test bug that is really an environment problem.
- Decision: on 2026-10-11, apart from overlapping runs in one checkout, the user said for development and release
  tooling: "fix everything small that's a legit bug, discard rest".
- Completion criteria: a rerun counts as a test failure only when the rerun's report shows the test itself ran and
  failed; otherwise the verdict is unclassified. If the fix is not small, record `discard` instead during execution.
  Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete; change `qskotuzousumonsppupuwqunlxolzztw`, bookmark
  `plan/dev-tooling-robustness-fixes/01-tooling-fixes`, [PR #1935](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/1935/changes).
  Per-test deterministic classification requires three rerun reports naming the selected test as failed; runner failures
  remain inconclusive.

## template-discovery-fails-permanently-once-reply-exceeds.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: partly correct. Template names are now capped at 128 bytes, so the finding's example no longer works, but
  per-template fields can reach 64 KiB, there is no total cap, and the catalog travels in one frame of at most 8 MiB, so
  about 130 near-maximum templates would break agents' template listing until some are deleted. Agents on any host can
  save templates, so an agent on one host could break template discovery for agents on every host.
- Decision: on 2026-10-11 the user said "fix SUPER cheap ones with complexity gate. and anything that means a security
  boundary is broken like helm being corrupted, or cross-host attackes, must not be silently discarded." This one is
  cross-host, so it is not discarded silently.
- Completion criteria: saving a template is refused when it would push the catalog past a total size that still fits a
  reply. If the cap is not cheap, bring it back to the user rather than discarding it. Remove this feedback file and its
  index entry.
- Execution: `pending`, waiting on the user: the cheap stored-name/fields cap cannot guarantee an agent listing fits its
  8 MiB reply. Per-row encoding and resolved host display names also count; SSH destinations are unbounded and host
  names can change after a template is saved. A save-time snapshot budget would leave later host changes outside the
  guarantee; bounding host display names would broaden the host-input contract. Recommend a separate byte-bounded
  listing/pagination plan, which can also handle existing oversized catalogs. No cap shipped; the original cross-host
  discovery risk remains unfixed. Feedback file and index entry retained.
- Outcome (2026-10-19, supersedes the above): `fix spec`.
- Decision (2026-10-19): on the cross-cutting triage page, the user accepted declaring a template catalog of that size
  out of scope, as the trash's scale was on 2026-10-16 (`trash-listing-exceeds-control-frame.md`). Every agent template
  write needs an approval card by default, so the catalog cannot grow that far silently.
- Completion criteria: SPEC_impl.md, next to the template catalog's description, says a catalog whose agent listing
  exceeds one reply frame (about 8 MiB, roughly 130 templates near the per-field cap) is outside the supported scale and
  agent template listing may then fail until templates are removed; the GUI is unaffected. No code change. Remove the
  feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `trtzwrmztxzuouvsuqlwwxpwtxtpuyww`, bookmark
  `plan/spec-scope-clarifications/03-template-catalog-scale`,
  [PR #2416](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2416/changes).

## tab-cleanup-blocks-status-sampling.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading. Automatic cleanup of an exited terminal tab runs inside the supervisor's periodic
  status pass and, once it has the session's lifecycle claim, waits for the whole close, both process sweeps and the
  5-second kill grace included, before agent screens are sampled. A tab whose leftover background process ignores TERM
  and HUP therefore leaves every session on that host with stale status for about 5 s per tab (about 20 s for four). The
  pane-death path waits the same way. SPEC.md "Waiting between operations on one host" forbids session status waiting on
  teardown grace periods, and `ticker-waits-on-lifecycle-claim.md` was fixed under the same rule.
- Decision: on 2026-10-11 the user accepted the recommendation, fix code with a complexity gate. It was held back from
  the no-question batch because the fix is a moderate concurrency change rather than a small one.
- Completion criteria: automatic tab cleanup runs as owned, bounded background work independent of status sampling,
  keeping each session's lifecycle guard and never starting a duplicate close job for the same tab. A regression test
  holds one tab's cleanup in its shutdown phase and proves another session still receives a fresh sample. If this needs
  significantly more than moving the close off the sampling pass (a new scheduler, a change to the lifecycle-claim
  design), stop and bring it back to the user unfixed. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete; jj change `rymmyqmqlsrsxywswpzuxusmkwqkvxou`; bookmark
  `plan/supervisor-and-test-followups/01-followups`; https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/1933/changes.

## uninstall-forgotten-success.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading. The GUI announces "Farhelm was removed" whenever the host leaves the list; the
  failure check that would withdraw the notice lives in the host row, which unmounts with it. When another window
  forgets the host while an uninstall from this window is failing, this window reports success while Farhelm stays
  installed. Host Remove exists only in the GUI, so the trigger needs two GUIs.
- Decision: on 2026-10-11 the user accepted the recommendation and added: "fix complexity gated. if the SPEC doesn't say
  already, we do not generally expend any serious complexity to support concurrent GUIs against the same helm." SPEC.md
  "One GUI at a time" already says that ("do not add significant machinery to keep concurrent GUIs consistent"), so no
  spec change is needed.
- Completion criteria: when the GUI never observed the uninstall finish, the notice says the outcome is unknown rather
  than that Farhelm was removed. If this needs more than a small change to the notice logic, stop and bring it back to
  the user unfixed. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `pending`, waiting on the user. The authorized small notice change cannot distinguish successful uninstall
  from another GUI's Remove: normal uninstall forgets the host and purges its result before completion can be observed,
  and accepting the request does not prove it finished. An observed-success flag would therefore turn ordinary success
  into unknown too, against the specified success notice. Options: accept the current concurrent-GUI residual
  (recommended under the one-GUI complexity policy); hedge every uninstall notice (changes normal-success wording); or
  separately authorize a correlated final result that survives forgetting the host (helm/API lifecycle work beyond this
  gate). No product change for this outcome; its original feedback remains queued. Scope review confirmed the gate
  return; the recorded Outcome is unchanged.
- Outcome (2026-10-19, supersedes the above): `other`.
- Decision (2026-10-19): on the cross-cutting triage page, the user accepted the recommended option: the residual is
  accepted under SPEC.md "One GUI at a time" ("do not add significant machinery to keep concurrent GUIs consistent"),
  since it needs a second GUI to remove the host while this one's uninstall is failing.
- Completion criteria: remove the feedback file and its index entry; no spec or code change.
- Execution: complete (queue cleanup during triage, per `review_feedback_queue/AGENTS.md`, "Lifecycle").

## restart-drain-skips-newly-published-conversation.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: likely by static reading at 4c9e9612, not reproduced; the mechanism is unchanged on main 6b237507. If the
  agent publishes its conversation report while Restart is collecting reports (a sub-second window, no fault needed),
  Restart resumes the previous conversation and the new report is discarded, so the session follows the previous
  conversation until the agent reports again. The newer conversation itself is not deleted.
- Decision: on 2026-10-14 the user set a principle for conversation tracking that decides this item and five others
  triaged with it: "Resuming the previous section in a brief window after a session has been replaced/conversation
  replaced whether by clicking or using /clear in an agent or similar is fine. For cases where the new session is
  long-term undiscoverable, that is a bug we mitigate with the pre-existing notification system when we don't learn of
  conversations. For the case where we have a conversation recorded and somehow behavior breaks underneath us and we
  stop updating but the user doesn't learn of it because we have what we believe is a valid conversation - that is
  "okay" in the sense that it's a reasonable consequene of a bug. We should avoid having those bugs, but the fact that
  we don't have a magical solution to that last case is not in and of itself a bug. SPEC should be updated." This item
  falls under the brief-window case.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md (Durability and resume, and the cleanup-and-resume exception under Lifecycle operations)
  states the three cases: Restart resuming the previous conversation in a brief window after a conversation switch is
  acceptable; a new conversation Farhelm never learns of is a defect, mitigated by the existing session-tracking
  notifications; and continuing to follow a recorded conversation after tracking silently stops updating is an accepted
  consequence of whatever bug stopped it, not a defect in itself. The spec change is made once, by whichever of the six

## quick-launch-acknowledgment-revives-previous-mark.md

- Outcome: `discard`.
- Assessment: confirmed by static ordering analysis, not reproduced. Marking template B (or binding a number key to it)
  and pressing the shortcut while that save is still in flight can launch the previously marked template A. It needs the
  helm to answer the shortcut's later preference read before applying the earlier save, and the save's acknowledgment to
  land before the template read finishes; separate requests to the helm carry no ordering guarantee, but the whole
  window is as long as one save, which is milliseconds against a local helm.
- Decision: on 2026-10-14 the user discarded this item and the three other quick-launch timing items: "this is fine. we
  are not worryed about it. we are not adding tons of complexity to account for multiple interfaces to the helm, and
  within the same interface this is a ridiculous condition that is impractical to reach, you'd have to click super fast
  AND the order of req/resp to helm would need to be out of order." After learning that the out-of-order part comes from
  independent HTTP requests rather than from any requirement, the user asked to "discard the relevant ones for now, but
  put a near term todo item to consider moving to an ordered transport instead of out of order http requests, with a
  reference to the specific issues that prompted this."
- Completion criteria: remove this feedback file and its index entry, without code or spec changes. The TODO.md Near
  term entry "Consider an ordered transport between the GUI and the helm" names this item.
- Execution: `complete`; feedback file and index entry removed under the recorded discard decision, without code, spec
  or filter changes. Change `vynrtwwrplpvrnusslrvvkstopkoutvw`, bookmark
  `plan/triage-highest-discards/01-discarded-findings`, [PR #2050](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2050/changes).

## codex-ancestor-clear-withdraws-unverified-resume.md

- Outcome: `discard`.
- Assessment: the control-flow exception is confirmed by reading; no real trigger was found. The harm needs a nested
  Codex's report to be adopted before the session's own Codex reports, then a `/clear` from the session's own Codex
  before its new transcript exists. In a fresh launch the session's own Codex reports first: Codex runs its start hook
  when the first prompt is submitted and adds the hook's output to the model's context (per the vendor documentation
  SPEC_impl.md cites), so the report is on disk before the agent can run any tool, `codex exec` included. The one
  documented route to a nested report coming first is a session that kept running across the upgrade that introduced
  Codex process pinning. Even then the consequence is losing a Resume that pointed at the nested Codex's conversation,
  the same as an ordinary `/clear` followed by Restart.
- Decision: on 2026-10-14 the user: "forget any edge case having to do with upgrading rom old versions if its combined
  with "super rare unlikely situation". its ok."
- Completion criteria: remove this feedback file and its index entry, without code or spec changes.
- Execution: `complete`; feedback file and index entry removed under the recorded discard decision, without code, spec
  or filter changes. Change `vynrtwwrplpvrnusslrvvkstopkoutvw`, bookmark

## interrupted-checkout-retains-evictable-cache-dependency.md

- Outcome: `other`.
- Assessment: likely by static reading, not reproduced. A managed checkout borrows data from the host's repository cache
  while git clones it and copies that data in at the end. If the clone is killed outright in between, the checkout looks
  usable but still borrows from the cache. Farhelm refuses to repeat an interrupted preparation and shows the failed
  stage in the session terminal, but a user who keeps working there anyway can later have the checkout's repository left
  incomplete by cache cleanup. Completed checkouts are unaffected.
- Decision: on 2026-10-14 the user: "I see, didn't realize the cache wasn't permanently referenced. so long as the user
  is told that it failed I woudlsay this is acceptable. not sure about generatrlization but lets put a filter for the
  specific issue". A filter for exactly this case, "Work continued in a checkout whose preparation was killed partway",
  was added to `review_feedback_queue/FILTER.md`, and the item was removed under the filter-match rule.
- Completion criteria: the filter exists, and this feedback file and its index entry are removed.
- Execution: complete, in the same change that recorded this triage session (filter added, file and index entry
  removed).

## guarded-choice-becomes-omp-yolo.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by static trace, not reproduced. In the New launcher, explicitly choosing Guarded for Claude,
  Codex, Grok or Muse and then switching the agent to OMP sets the mode to YOLO: the switch clears a permission equal to
  the previous agent's default, and OMP's own default, YOLO, fills in. OMP supports Guarded (`--approval-mode write`).
  The launcher shows YOLO before Launch, and a host set to ask before YOLO still asks. OMP is the only agent that offers
  Guarded while defaulting to YOLO; Claude, Codex, Grok and Muse already default to Guarded, Pi and OpenCode offer only
  YOLO, Cursor offers YOLO or custom flags, and Goose offers YOLO, approve, smart approve and chat but no mode Farhelm
  calls Guarded.
- Decision: on 2026-10-14 the user first asked for automatic changes toward a more dangerous mode to be very hard to
  miss: "whenever the permission modes changes in the direction of MORE dangerous, we visually highlight it in a way
  that is very hard to miss ... some kind of animation or similar for a second or two along with a message card
  temporarily saying it changed because you switched agents." From mockups of five options they chose the banner: "C
  looks best to me but can we be clear that the reason is that guarded is not supported by that agent type?" Told that
  OMP does support Guarded, they decided: "if OMP now supports guarded then we should change the default to be that
  instead", "and make sure we do this for ALL agents if any other agent currently both supports guraded yet somehow yolo
  is the default", and "this shoudl also be a SPEC rule: For any agent that supports guarded, guarded is always the

  recognition, so a Guarded OMP session stuck on an approval prompt shows no waiting alert, and gave this direction
  after that.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md states the rule that for any agent that supports Guarded, Guarded is the default (the

  the upgrade path stays intact. When switching agents in the launcher changes the permission mode to a more dangerous

## mouse-reporting-drag-activates-file-link.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main, not reproduced in a browser. Every terminal link activation (web URL,
  program-emitted OSC 8 link, printed file path) treats a press and release on the same link as a click, and the only
  drag guard is a non-empty local selection. With mouse reporting on, the terminal makes no local selection, so a drag
  that starts and ends inside one link opens the URL or downloads the file, and with the native modifier held also opens
  an admitted `.md`/`.txt` save. Web links are affected too, not only file links. SPEC.md's file-link and link-opening
  rules treat the click as the authorization, and a drag is not a click.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user ruled the explicit click "not a hard line but all of these are nice to fix if it's
  not terribly complicated, ESPECIALLY the 'dragging across a link' that seems super POLA violating", then chose "fix
  code, with complexity gate. can't turn large/very complex." The assessed fix is small: remember where the primary
  press landed and ignore activation when the release is more than a few pixels away, in one check shared by web, OSC 8
  and file-path activation.
- Completion criteria: a drag across any terminal link, with or without mouse reporting, neither opens a URL nor
  transfers or opens a file; a plain click still does. Regression coverage drives a mouse-reporting program in both
  browser engines. If the fix turns out large or very complex, stop and return the item to the user rather than build
  it. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: jj change `pwnymqroxtxwzlxowsmkxyxntsulzznq`, bookmark `plan/terminal-link-safety/01-drag-click`,
  [PR #2078](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2078/changes).

## os-trusted-proxy-can-read-feedback.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed as deliberate by reading; no interception set up. Feedback uses the OS certificate store and
  system proxy on purpose, so it works behind proxies that use their own certificates. An interception proxy the OS
  trusts can therefore read feedback. That trust was configured by the user or their machine's administrator.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user: "all these findings should be ignored. my only hesitation in adjusting the spec is i
  don't know how to convey where the line is. Like we want to not be unreasonable and take reasonable precautions
  against likely real life mistakes, but something like the interception proxy is just crazy insane over zealous
  security." They then agreed to this principle: Farhelm defends against what an attached host or an agent's output can
  do, and against mistakes a user plausibly makes in ordinary use of Farhelm or their machine. It does not defend
  against conditions the user, or whoever administers their machine, deliberately set up outside Farhelm (their shell
  environment, the OS certificate store and proxies, symlinks or files they reshape by hand); it takes those as the
  user's intent. The test is whether a reasonable user would hit the trigger by accident. This never relaxes the
  remote-host boundary.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md generalizes its existing deliberate-versus-accidental interference paragraph into that
  principle, with the OS-trusted proxy and the retargeted symlink as examples, and states that feedback's
  confidentiality does not extend to proxies the OS trusts. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `mzovvwlvzomsnowvztyzvrknmomtkorm`, bookmark
  `plan/deliberate-setup-spec/01-proxy-principle`; PR https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2075/changes. The shared
  principle and proxy limit are specified here; the retargeted-symlink example follows in the next outcome's PR.

## checkout-recovery-requester-not-bound-to-host.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main, not exploited. The key that lets a retried agent create into a managed
  checkout finish an attempt the user already approved is built from the asking session's id, which the remote host
  supplies, and the agent's key. Another attached host that knows or guesses both can repeat the request and finish the
  first host's approved attempt without an approval of its own. SPEC.md limits that replay to the session that asked.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user chose `fix code` after being told it is small: include the helm-known host of the
  requesting connection in the key at both call sites. Retries in flight across the upgrade stop matching and are asked
  about again, the same accepted effect as when keys were first scoped to the asking session.
- Completion criteria: a keyed create or clone repeated from a different host never reconciles with another host's
  attempt and goes through ordinary approval; a retry from the same host and session still finishes its approved
  attempt. Covered by a regression test. Remove this feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; create and clone retry keys now bind the helm-known requesting host, asking session and raw key
  with a fixed-length digest. A regression covers approval, same-host recovery and a second host repeating the request.
  Change `txmwnsww`, bookmark `plan/checkout-recovery-host-binding/01-host-bound-key`,
  [PR #2086](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2086/changes).

## uninstall-stale-socket-loses-private-client.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: an uninstall run can stop after Farhelm's private directory (which holds its private tmux) has been
  removed but before the host is forgotten: the helm stops, or the registry deletion fails. Every Retry after that then
  fails on a host whose supervisor and tmux are already gone, and the host stays listed with a tmux "not found" error.
  The cause is the stop step's shell script (`SystemBackend::stop` in
  `crates/farhelm-helm/src/provisioning/backend.rs`). It runs the frozen client whenever `stat` finds the socket path,
  and only the "no such file" stat result is excused. The repository says tmux leaves its socket file behind when the
  server exits; see `kill_tmux_server`'s docs in `crates/farhelm-teststate/src/lib.rs` and the "tmux can leave a stale
  socket" comment in the provisioning test. So the socket is normally still there after the first run's successful stop,
  and the plan's client, `<lib>/tmux` on hosts without an acceptable host tmux, is what the next step deletes. Verified
  by code reading. The existing regression in `crates/farhelm-helm/src/provisioning.rs` deletes the socket by hand
  before its missing-client check, which hides exactly this case. Settled by: SPEC_impl.md "UNINSTALL is the third
  operation…": "An absent server skips this cleanup, including a retry after the lib directory was removed; any other
  tmux failure leaves the host listed so uninstall can be retried." The spec also says "a failed run continues from
  wherever it stopped".
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in the stop script, once the
  server is proven gone or told to exit, unlink the socket file (`rm -f -- "$socket"`) in the same shell. That covers a
  successful `kill-server` and the excused "no server running on …" (ECONNREFUSED) result. A later lib-gone retry then
  sees the path absent and skips. Then change the regression so it no longer removes the socket by hand. It should
  assert that the first stop leaves no socket, and that a retry with a removed client is `Skipped`. Complexity gate:
  confined to the stop script in `backend.rs` and its test in `provisioning.rs`, with no new provisioning action, plan
  field, API or persisted state. Never unlink after an unexcused tmux failure. Hosts already stranded by older releases
  (lib gone, stale socket) are out of scope. They fall under the FILTER.md upgrade filter, which applies only when an
  older release is combined with a rare interruption. If a correct fix needs a socket probe that does not use the
  client, a plan reordering, or a new action, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: after a successful or excused stop, no socket file remains, and an uninstall retried after the
  lib directory was removed skips the tmux cleanup and goes on to forget the host. The updated real-user-manager
  regression covers the stale-socket and missing-client combination without manual socket removal. Remove the feedback
  file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `nyxlxnvknlvtnlotvvnozkytxourqkmp`, bookmark
  `plan/remote-uninstall-fixes/02-retry-socket`; [PR #2100](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2100/changes).

## teststate-socket-probe-blocks-sweep.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: test runs on a machine with an abandoned, wedged private tmux server whose listen backlog has filled can
  hang before any fixture starts. `kill_tmux_server` in `crates/farhelm-teststate/src/lib.rs` first does a blocking
  `UnixStream::connect`. On Linux that call blocks indefinitely on a full Unix-socket backlog, and it runs before the
  five-second child deadline and outside the thirty-second pass budget. The sweep runs synchronously from
  `tempdir_with_sweep`, so every later Rust fixture, and the browser stack's startup sweep, would stall. Verified by
  code reading. The reviewer demonstrated the blocking syscall on a private listener, but not against a real tmux
  server. Settled by: this is not SPEC text. It is the crate's own documented contract on `TMUX_KILL_DEADLINE`: "the
  sweep must never hang: a wedged server … can accept the connection and simply never answer, and one such entry must
  not block every subsequent harness startup". The FILTER.md "hung private tmux server" filter does not match, because
  the consequence is harness startup on the whole machine, not one supervisor's host.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: make the preliminary probe a
  nonblocking connect (`libc` is already a dependency). Only `ECONNREFUSED`/`ENOENT` count as absent.
  `EAGAIN`/`EINPROGRESS` or any other result falls through to the existing deadline-bound `tmux kill-server` child,
  which already preserves the directory on timeout. Add a regression with a private listener whose backlog is full,
  showing the sweep returns promptly and keeps the directory. Complexity gate: confined to `kill_tmux_server` and its
  tests in `farhelm-teststate`, with no change to sweep policy, budgets or directory selection. If a nonblocking probe
  cannot be done without a new dependency or platform-specific branching beyond `libc`, stop and return the item.
- Completion criteria: a sweep over a directory whose socket has a full backlog completes within the existing budgets
  and preserves that directory. The new test is bounded and annotated per the test-sleep checker. Remove the feedback
  file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `uuomyvuouqyt`, bookmark `plan/rust-test-portability/06-socket-probe`,
  [PR #2103](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2103/changes).

## default-approval-reset-renews-retry-key.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: In the new-session dialog, applying a template whose permission is an explicit reset
  (`"permissions": null`) leaves the launcher's permission choice unset. The first press of Launch then never settles on
  a stable request key. On a host that asks before YOLO launches (OMP/Goose default to YOLO), confirming the YOLO
  question just brings it back again, so the template cannot be launched. On any host, including guarded-default
  Claude/Codex, retrying an unchanged launch after a lost reply sends a new key and can start a second session. Verified
  by code reading (no browser run): the initial selection in the submit handler of
  `crates/farhelm-ui/src/list/create_form.rs` is passed through `launch_composer::normalized_permissions`, but the
  post-mint re-read inside the mint loop builds `LaunchSelection { permissions: *structured_permissions.peek(), .. }`
  without that call. The template reset path (`structured_permissions.set(None)` in template application) makes the two
  differ, so each submit mints again. Settled by: the submit path's own documented contract in `create_form.rs` says the
  key is "Minted at first submit, reused by every later submit of the same" binding, and the re-read exists only to
  catch a real edit during the mint. SPEC.md, the idempotency rules around "An optional idempotency key makes retries
  safe" and the YOLO confirmation rules ("An agent launch counts as YOLO when its stored permission is custom or YOLO,
  including omitted permissions ...") assume a confirmed or retried unchanged launch keeps its key. Nothing in the spec
  accepts an unanswerable YOLO loop.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in the post-mint structured
  re-read in `create_form.rs`, normalize `permissions` with
  `crate::launch_composer::normalized_permissions(harness, ...)`, the same helper the initial selection uses. Best done
  by having both sites share one small selection-building helper so they cannot drift again. Complexity gate: confined
  to the structured-selection construction in `create_form.rs`'s submit path, plus an optional shared helper beside it.
  No change to the protocol, to template application, to `launch_composer` normalization or to key storage. If the fix
  appears to need changes to how a reset template stores its permission, or to server-side key matching, stop and return
  the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: after a null-permission template, an unchanged Launch binds one key across the mint re-read and
  across unchanged retries, and confirming a YOLO question launches instead of asking again. Add a regression test, a
  unit test on the shared selection helper or a focused browser route fixture: a null-reset OMP or Goose template
  completes YOLO consent with one request key, and a null-reset guarded-default template keeps its key across an
  unchanged retry. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `xuwwmqtpspxsvzomkullwxwrswtnxypx`, bookmark `plan/launcher-fixes/01-retry-key`,
  [PR #2160](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2160/changes).

## failed-feedback-cleanup-loses-evidence.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: In the release brick test's coordinator, cleaning up the final P0 pair after a failed or could-not-run P1
  feedback check deletes both guests without checking that P1's recorded evidence files are still intact. If the
  exported screenshot was lost or altered, the guest, which may be the only remaining copy, is deleted anyway. Confirmed
  by code reading of `releasing/mac-vm-test/brick_test.py`. In `cleanup`,
  `retained = self.verdict(p1) == 'pass' or all(result['status'] != 'pass' ...)`, and `verdict()` only hashes artifacts
  for results whose status is `pass` (nonpassing results return before the hash loop). Every recorded result carries
  `sha256` for its bound references (`record`). The finding cites a synthetic-substrate reproduction (run ac7dd320-...).
  Whether a real guest still holds evidence the export lacks is unverified, but the missing gate is what the procedure
  forbids. Settled by: `releasing/mac-vm-test/RECIPE.md` step 4: "Retain failure evidence before cleanup; a P1 failure
  ... does not prevent ordinary cleanup of this pair". BRICK-TEST.md: "A valid P1 product failure or unavailable
  observation does not require retaining the clones ...; its evidence and verdict remain saved." The existing
  `test_lost_p1_success_evidence_preserves_guests_until_recovered` already enforces this for a passing P1.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in `cleanup`, require for
  nonpassing P1 results that every recorded `sha256` reference still hashes to its digest before treating P1 as

## paste-guide-overstates-control-byte-protection.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.

  (`website/src/content/docs/docs/using/work-in-a-session.mdx`) says "Pasted text has hidden control characters removed,
  so a paste cannot type keystrokes you did not see." The implementation (`sanitizePastedText` in
  `crates/farhelm-ui/assets/term-bytes.js`) removes only ESC bytes and the embedded bracketed-paste end marker. Ctrl-C,
  Ctrl-D and other control bytes still reach the program, so a reader can trust a protection that does not exist.

  section) says "A user-initiated paste intentionally sends the pasted content to the selected terminal". The
  sanitizer's documented purpose is to keep pasted text inside the terminal's bracketed-paste frame. The spec promises
  no broader control-byte filtering, so the guide must match the implementation, not the other way round.

  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: rewrite that one sentence to
  state the real protection, for example that pasted text cannot break out of the terminal's paste framing because

  `website/EDITORIAL_RULES.md` and the scode-voice skill. Complexity gate: docs-only, that sentence (and an identical

  the docs Overview page or intro SVGs. If the maintainer's editorial rules call for a broader paste explanation,

## native-download-collision-exceeds-filename-limit.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on current main. When the desktop app saves a terminal file link into Downloads
  and the name is taken, `candidates()` (`crates/farhelm-helm/src/downloads.rs`) appends ` (n)` to the full stem without
  shortening it. For a basename near the 255-byte component limit, every numbered candidate exceeds the limit, and
  `StagedStream::publish_no_clobber` (`crates/farhelm-supervisor/src/files.rs`) retries only on `AlreadyExists`. The
  save then fails the same way on every retry until the user renames or removes the existing file. Not reproduced. The
  trigger (a basename of about 250 bytes or more) is rare. Settled by: SPEC.md terminal file links: "The desktop app
  saves into Downloads under a unique name and shows where it went". SPEC_impl.md: "Atomic no-clobber publication uses
  `report.pdf`, `report (1).pdf`, and so on, preserving the final extension."
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in `candidates()`, when
  `stem + " (n)" + extension` would exceed 255 bytes, truncate the stem at a UTF-8 character boundary so the candidate
  fits, keeping the extension and the numbered suffix. The unsuffixed first candidate is unchanged. Complexity gate:
  confined to `candidates()` (and its unit tests) in `crates/farhelm-helm/src/downloads.rs`. Use a fixed 255-byte
  component limit, with no per-filesystem `pathconf` query, no new error handling in `publish_no_clobber` and no other
  naming changes. If the extension alone leaves no room, keep failing with the existing error. If more is needed, stop
  and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: a second save of a file with a 251-byte stem plus `.pdf` publishes as a truncated stem with
  ` (1).pdf` within 255 bytes. Ordinary names keep `name (n).ext` unchanged. Multi-byte names are never split inside a
  character. Unit tests cover these cases. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: jj change `rqvntlwpoovrykqzlvqyolzzvouunlzq`, bookmark `plan/download-long-name-copies/01-name-limit`;
  [PR #2114](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2114/changes).

## missing-ca-bundle-blocks-helm-start.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: on a Linux helm machine with no CA certificates package, the whole helm (web UI and every host view) exits
  at startup instead of starting with release downloads and feedback unavailable. This happens even with `--payload-dir`
  or on a developer build, neither of which downloads anything. Verified by code reading on current main:
  `production_payloads` (`crates/farhelm-helm/src/provisioning/payloads.rs`) evaluates `release_client()?` eagerly. With
  no CA roots, reqwest's client build fails, and the error propagates through `ProvisioningService::production`
  (`provisioning/service.rs`) and `AppState::new` (`lib.rs`) out of helm startup. Not reproduced. Settled by: SPEC.md
  does not address the case directly. The maintainer-approved design note that #1909 added beside the reqwest dependency
  in `Cargo.toml` records the accepted behavior: "on a Linux machine with no CA bundle, building ANY reqwest client
  fails ... The helm survives it: the feedback forwarder logs the error and reports that it cannot send, and
  provisioning fails with 'building the release download HTTP client'." The code contradicts that note. There is also a
  precedent decision, `embedded-payload-cleanup-blocks-helm-start.md` (`fix code`, complete): provisioning-side failures
  that do not need to block the helm must not stop it from starting. Caveat: the settling text is that note and the
  precedent, not SPEC.md itself.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in `payloads.rs`, build the HTTP
  client only for the arms that download (`PayloadSelection::Release` and the release-build `Default` arm). If the build
  fails, return a refusing `PayloadSource`, like the existing `UnreleasedPayloads`, whose `path()` fails with the
  client-build error under the existing context ("building the release download HTTP client"). The `Directory`,
  `NoPayloads` and `UnreleasedPayloads` arms must never construct a client. `production_payloads_with_key` can take the
  client as a `Result`, or as a closure, to keep the tests' injection seam. Complexity gate: stays in
  `provisioning/payloads.rs` (plus test call sites of `production_payloads_with_key`). No change to the TLS/root-store
  choice in `Cargo.toml`, no new API or persisted state, and no change to the feedback forwarder. If startup still fails
  somewhere else on a client build (another eager reqwest client in helm startup), or the fix needs more than a refusing
  source and lazy construction, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: a helm whose release client cannot be built still starts and serves the UI. Provisioning through
  a download source reports the client-build error. `--payload-dir` and developer builds never attempt the build. Add a
  focused unit test that injects a failing client result and checks both the refusing source and the non-downloading
  arms. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: jj change `ypquprnnrvsqlrpsvvlnvtrutrxvplto`, bookmark `plan/helm-start-without-ca-bundle/01-lazy-client`;
  draft PR https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2116/changes.

## resume-docs-promise-newest-conversation.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: the docs website tells readers that after `/clear`, Restart no longer resumes the old conversation
  (`website/src/content/docs/docs/agents/codex.md`, the `/clear` bullet). It also says reporters make a restart resume
  the conversation "you were actually in ... instead of the one you threw away"
  (`website/src/content/docs/docs/how-it-works/agent-hook-injection.md`, opening paragraph). The spec now accepts that
  Restart may resume the earlier conversation within a brief window after a switch, then continue with it. A reader
  relying on the docs is promised more than Farhelm guarantees. Verified by reading both pages and SPEC.md on current
  main. The commit that changed the spec (#2038, `84520906`) touched no website page. Settled by: SPEC.md, the
  "Confirmed 2026-10-14" paragraph: "after a session or its conversation is replaced ... Restart resuming the previous
  conversation within a brief window is acceptable, and so is Farhelm then continuing with the conversation Restart
  resumed". `website/EDITORIAL_RULES.md` "What the site is not": "A page must agree with them."
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: reword the Codex `/clear` bullet
  and the hook-injection page's opening sentence. They should say that Restart resumes the conversation Farhelm last
  learned of, and that Farhelm learns the new one once Codex has finished its next reply. Restarting before then can
  bring back the earlier conversation. Follow the editorial rules' vocabulary. Complexity gate: docs-only, confined to
  those two pages (plus any other non-Overview page found making the same absolute promise). No new section or page. No

## cached-launch-error-overrides-completed-stop.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: Stop a session while its checkout is still being cloned or its post-clone hook is running. If the Stop
  commits before the ticker's launch-evidence batch, the supervisor records "exited, stopped". The status reply still
  shows Error, and keeps showing it until a relaunch or a supervisor reload. Verified by code reading, not reproduced.
  In `observe_entries` (`service/ticker.rs`) the observer caches the preparation-failure detail in `run.launch_error`
  before calling `transition_many`. The store refuses `SentinelError` against a stop-annotated `Exited` (`store.rs`,
  `Transition::apply`). `mirror_committed_outcome` (`service/hints.rs`) clears `launch_error` only for a committed
  `Error`. The status reply builder (`service/status.rs`, around the `launch_error` override) then lets the cached
  detail win over the durable annotated exit. Later observations skip launch reads for annotated exits
  (`sentinel_could_still_apply` in `launch_artifacts.rs`), so nothing repairs it. Not covered by FILTER.md: the trigger
  is a successful ordinary Stop, not a crash or a partly failed operation, and the wrong status persists, which excludes
  the rare-glitch filter. Settled by: SPEC.md session statuses: "A user-initiated stop yields exited with an
  annotation". SPEC_impl.md (ticker/list paragraph): "Found but uncommitted launch errors stay in generation-local
  memory for replies". A rejected error is not merely uncommitted; the store's documented precedence makes it
  uncommittable.
- Decision: on 2026-10-15 the user delegated this class of decision: "for everything that's left in any bucket: please
  assess which ones are CLEARLY settled by the spec, don't need my judgement, and can be fixed without significant
  complexity or scope creep. triage those as 'fix code' with explicit complexity gates." A fresh-context pre-triage
  review, checked by the triaging session, classed this finding that way. Planned fix: in the status reply, apply the
  cached `launch_error` only while `sentinel_could_still_apply` holds for the mirrored outcome, i.e. never over a
  stop-annotated `Exited` (an `Error` outcome already wins). Optionally also clear the cache in
  `mirror_committed_outcome` when the committed outcome makes a sentinel inapplicable. The read-side guard alone covers
  the concurrent-publication ordering. Complexity gate: confined to `service/status.rs` and, optionally,
  `service/hints.rs`. No store, protocol or schema change, and no change to the store's transition rules. If it turns
  out to need reordering the ticker's cache-then-commit sequence or new synchronization, stop and return the item to the
  maintainer.
- Completion criteria: a session whose durable outcome is a stop-annotated exit is listed as exited (stopped) even when
  an observer cached a launch or preparation error for that generation. A cached error still shows for Running,
  StopRequested, unannotated `Exited` and `Interrupted` outcomes. Add a unit test that seeds both the cache and an
  annotated outcome and checks the reply. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `zupllqoyrwsp`, bookmark `plan/stopped-session-launch-error/01-stopped-status`.
  [PR #2117](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2117/changes).

## menu-request-overrides-independent-focus.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: mechanism confirmed on current main; the trigger was not reproduced. When an arrow key is pressed in an
  open session row menu, the next item is computed from the position of the last keyboard step the menu itself
  requested, ahead of the actually focused item (`crates/farhelm-ui/src/menu_panel.rs`, `menu_step_origin`). The item
  focus handlers (`crates/farhelm-ui/src/list/row.rs`) update only the focused position and never clear that request. So
  if focus moves inside the open menu without a keyboard step (a pointer press that focuses an item without activating
  it, or a screen reader moving focus), the next arrow steps from the old position, not from the focused item. That can
  move focus to Delete unexpectedly; deleting still needs Enter or Space on it. The request precedence exists to fix a
  real race (an older in-flight focus request landing after a newer key press), so the fix must keep that. SPEC_impl.md
  (row menu "Keyboard") says arrows step from the current command, so this is outside the specification.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user asked to triage this as `fix code` if it can be fixed easily at the GUI level. It
  can, but not as trivially as the trash item: the fix has to tell apart the menu's own delayed focus results from
  independent focus moves.
- Completion criteria: after focus moves to a menu item independently (not as the result of a request the menu itself
  made), the next arrow steps from that item; a burst of arrow presses still advances once per press. Candidate
  approaches: clear the pending request on a pointer press inside the panel, and/or on a focus-in at a position the menu
  has no in-flight request for. Regression tests for both the independent-move case and the existing burst race.
  Complexity gate: confined to `menu_panel.rs` and the menu wiring in the rows that use it; if it needs a new
  cross-component focus mechanism or regresses the burst behaviour, stop and return the item. Remove the feedback file
  and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `nurzyvxqoxvrqszsxwuuwrpokmkptlqr`, bookmark
  `plan/menu-arrows-follow-focus/01-focus-landing`, [PR #2176](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2176/changes).

## checkout-retry-reuses-fresh-helm-host-namespace.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed from code on current main; not reproduced end to end. When an agent asks for a new session in a
  fresh managed checkout on another host, the helm derives the retry key it sends to the target supervisor from the
  asking host's numeric registry row ID, the asking session ID and the agent's raw key
  (`crates/farhelm-helm/src/agent_requests.rs`, `asker_scoped_intent_key`). The target stores a permanent reservation
  under that opaque key and checks only the key and the request digest; it knows nothing about which helm or host asked
  (`crates/farhelm-supervisor/src/service/core.rs`). Row IDs are SQLite AUTOINCREMENT values local to one database, and
  the helm has no durable identity of its own. So after the registry is lost and the target is re-registered with a
  fresh one (SPEC.md, "Topology"), a different host given the same row ID can present A's exact key, session ID and
  request, and get A's earlier answer back. If A's approved attempt was interrupted before its session started, it can
  instead relaunch A's approved launch on the target with no new approval. The helm does not verify the forwarded
  session ID, but session IDs are random UUIDs, so this needs a lying or compromised supervisor on B that knows A's
  tuple, not an honest collision. B cannot choose new launch contents. SPEC.md limits the managed-checkout retry
  exemption to "the session, on the host, that asked"; nothing accepts the cross-registry case. The related
  `checkout-recovery-requester-not-bound-to-host.md` outcome fixed collisions within one registry only. Bucket note: the
  narrow preconditions and the small gain make `highest` debatable, but the outcome does not depend on the bucket.
  Unverified: whether the target's display name after recovery matches the original host name in the request digest, and
  that re-provisioning leaves the target's reservations untouched (reasoned from the specification, not traced).
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user asked to triage this as `fix code` if it is clearly a bug that needs no judgement and
  is reasonably straightforward to fix. It is: the replay breaks a rule SPEC.md states, and the fix is small and
  confined to the helm.
- Completion criteria: give each helm database a durable random namespace and include it in the scoped retry key, so
  keys minted by different registries never match. Helm-only; no wire-protocol or supervisor change, since the target
  treats the key as opaque. A helm.db schema migration adds the namespace. To avoid re-asking for in-flight retries
  after upgrade, existing databases may keep a null namespace (hashing as today), with only newly created databases
  minting one; a recovered registry is always a new database. Do not swap the row ID for the host's install identity:
  approvals deliberately follow the host entry across adoption (SPEC.md). Update the key unit test and expected-key
  assertions, and add a regression test showing that the same row ID, session ID, raw key and request under two
  different helm databases produce different scoped keys. Complexity gate: if this needs supervisor or wire changes, or
  changes how approvals follow a host entry, stop and return the item. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
  Superseded in part, later on 2026-10-16: while scheduling, the user chose to give every helm database a namespace,
  existing ones included, instead of the optional null-namespace path above, preferring the simpler end-state code and
  accepting that keyed retries in flight across the upgrade are treated as new requests once.
- Execution: complete in jj change `rwyskqpzslmnqpnlqmmvwrwmnpwwqols`, bookmark
  `plan/checkout-retry-helm-namespace/01-helm-namespace`,
  [PR #2172](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2172/changes).

## download-cancel-retains-pending-admission.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main; not run, and memory growth was not measured. When a terminal file
  download is cancelled before it starts (for example the browser drops the download request while the helm is still
  asking the supervisor to begin it), the helm's guard in `crates/farhelm-helm/src/client/downloads.rs` retires the
  download route and sends AbortDownload, but never removes the pending `BeginDownload` request. The supervisor handles
  AbortDownload by dropping the route, which aborts its task (`crates/farhelm-supervisor/src/service/downloads.rs`); if
  that happens before the task sends DownloadStarted or a refusal, no reply ever comes. The helm removes a pending
  request only on a reply or on connection teardown, so each such cancellation leaves one entry until the host
  reconnects. The helm's download HTTP handler awaits `begin_download` directly, so ordinary browser cancellation
  reaches this. Spec: SPEC_impl.md, "Supervisor metadata retention and nonresponse": "This exception does not excuse
  unbounded accumulation during ordinary operation with a correctly behaving supervisor." The supervisor here behaves as
  designed: an aborted download is deliberately not answered. The earlier decision on
  `cancelled-request-leaks-pending-entry.md` covers selectively nonresponding supervisors and chose not to add general
  cancellation cleanup, so it does not cover this case, and the fix must stay specific to downloads.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user asked which untriaged items meet both "it's CLEARLY A problem to be fixed according
  to the spec, it needs no judgement from me" and "it's a reasonably straightforward fix that doesn't cause complexity
  or scope creep", reviewed the session's assessment that this item meets both, and said "record triage outcome the ones
  that met criteria." Planned fix: either the helm retires the pending `BeginDownload` entry when the download guard is
  dropped before a reply (a drop-time cleanup task like the existing `cancel_download`; a late reply to an id that is no
  longer pending is already dropped silently), or the supervisor answers an AbortDownload whose download has not replied
  yet. Complexity gate: download-specific. No change to the shared request path's semantics, no general cancellation
  cleanup, no new timeouts or quotas. If the fix needs either, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: cancelling a download admission before the supervisor replies leaves no pending request behind on
  the live connection. A regression cancels admission in that window and asserts the pending entry is gone; run it
  through the recorder. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `olusylrnlvlouvtpwyqtlrzylxzxvwsk`, bookmark `plan/download-cancel-pending-entry/01-retire-entry`;
  draft PR [#2197](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2197/changes).

## bare-cache-fetch-conflicts-with-explicit-git-policy.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed. When a host's Git is configured with `safe.bareRepository=explicit`, every session launched
  into a fresh GitHub checkout fails at its clone stage. The supervisor fetches into its per-host bare repository cache
  with `git ... -C <cache> fetch` (`crates/farhelm-supervisor/src/launch.rs`, the shim's cache fetch); `-C` makes Git
  discover the bare repository, which that policy refuses, while `--git-dir` names it explicitly and is allowed. A cache
  failure fails the clone stage with no fallback (SPEC.md), so no checkout, hook or agent runs. The reviewer's
  recorder-backed probe on Git 2.43.0 returned 128 for the `-C` fetch and 0 for the `--git-dir` fetch. That fetch is the
  only place the supervisor reaches the cache with `-C`; `git clone --reference <cache>` passes the cache as a path; a
  pre-triage check on 2026-10-15 reported that it also succeeds under the policy, which this session did not repeat.
  SPEC_impl.md prescribes the current command line literally
  (`git -c gc.autoDetach=false -c maintenance.autoDetach=false -C <cache> fetch --prune ...`), so the code matches the
  spec and the spec's command line changes with it. Neither spec addresses this Git setting. No Planned item, BUGS.md
  entry or filter covers it.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user asked which untriaged items meet both "it's CLEARLY A problem to be fixed according
  to the spec, it needs no judgement from me" and "it's a reasonably straightforward fix that doesn't cause complexity
  or scope creep", reviewed the session's assessment that this item meets both, with the caveat that SPEC_impl.md's
  command line changes too, and said "record triage outcome the ones that met criteria." Principle for the spec: the
  supervisor names its own bare cache explicitly, so a host's restrictive bare-repository policy keeps working and is
  never overridden. Planned fix: select the cache with `--git-dir <cache>` instead of `-C <cache>` in the shim's fetch,
  update the exact-argv test, and update the command line in SPEC_impl.md with half a sentence on why. Complexity gate:
  that fetch's arguments, its tests, and the SPEC_impl.md command block. Never relax the user's policy (no
  `-c safe.bareRepository=all`), and do not audit other Git safety settings. If the clone or another cache step also
  fails under the policy and needs more than naming the cache explicitly, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: a fresh-checkout launch succeeds on a host whose Git sets `safe.bareRepository=explicit`. A
  real-Git regression in the launch tests' isolated Git environment sets the policy and runs the shim's cache fetch and
  clone, asserting both succeed; run it through the recorder. SPEC_impl.md shows the new command line. Remove the
  feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `vxsopzwyronvsrynsuymupxzwosykpqt`, bookmark `plan/bare-cache-explicit-git-dir/01-git-dir`; draft PR
  [#2199](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2199/changes).

## claude-trust-publish-after-lock-takeover.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: partly correct. With the opt-in Claude trust setting on, Farhelm edits Claude's settings file under the
  lock Claude uses for it. The writer checks the lock's age (under 4 s), the lock's identity and the file's identity,
  then renames its replacement into place with no further guard, so a writer frozen past Claude's stale-lock threshold
  between those checks and the rename can overwrite a Claude save made in that gap. That window is inherent to a
  mkdir-style lock with a stale timeout, and Claude's own writers have the same exposure. Unverified: Claude 2.1.300's
  actual stale-lock takeover and timing (the vendor binary was not inspected), whether any realistic stall lands in a
  window of a few system calls, and what a lost Claude update can hold. SPEC.md's caveats name Claude's unlocked exit
  save and future vendor changes, not this trigger.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user chose to document it as an accepted limit, saying: "This was an intentional
  risk/trade-off during design and is intentiona[l]." Principle for the spec: Farhelm follows Claude's advisory lock the
  way Claude's own writers do, so a Farhelm writer stalled past Claude's stale-lock threshold can lose an update in
  either direction; this is an accepted trade-off of editing Claude's file, not a defect to narrow.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md's Claude trust caveats (and SPEC_impl.md's matching passage, if it lists the accepted
  vendor races) state that limit beside the unlocked exit-save race. No code change. Remove the feedback file and its
  index entry.
- Execution: change `koumoqkvlznlxmxoooszpvtryyklmloo`, bookmark `plan/triage-spec-rules-oct16/01-claude-lock-limit`;
  draft PR [#2193](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2193/changes).

## claude-trust-settings-misses-invalidation.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main; no browser reproduction. Settings loads the two shared Claude trust
  values (the automatic-trust switch and the hint dismissal) once and reloads only after its own save, while the hint
  band above the terminal reloads on every session update. An already-open Settings in one window therefore keeps
  showing the old values after another window changes them, until it is reopened. Toggling then saves the user's chosen
  value, so nothing changes against their intent. Only another GUI can change these values, the other Settings sections
  also load once, and SPEC_impl.md says other clients' Settings choices are picked up on reload. The conflict is the
  trust section's sentence "Other clients observe saved changes through the normal invalidation feed", which sits in the
  hint-band paragraph and reads as covering the dialog too.
