  why these things keep coming up. Can we strengthen the "one gui at a time" thing somehow to avoid this and similar
  things constantly raised? This should just be triaged w/o my judgement or not [filed] to begin with by agents."
  Principle for the spec: SPEC.md "One GUI at a time" says explicitly that with several GUIs open, a view already open
  in one GUI need not reflect a change saved from another until it is reopened or the page reloads, unless the spec
  names that view's live update explicitly; a finding whose only trigger is a second GUI showing older state is covered
  by that rule, not a defect. The existing limits still hold: correct behavior alongside the command line and agents,
  the session view's multi-client rules, and destructive prompts' preconditions.
- Completion criteria: the trust section's sentence says invalidation updates the hint band and Settings shows current
  values when opened; "One GUI at a time" gains the stale-open-view rule above, worded so a reviewer or triager can
  apply it without asking the maintainer. No code change. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `rvvxoonykyvylpnulwrzyykqtuxyysqr`, bookmark `plan/triage-spec-rules-oct16/02-stale-gui-views`;
  draft PR [#2195](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2195/changes).

## replace-retries-replay-settled-create-failure.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main; no runtime reproduction. Plain Replace keeps its request identity after
  any refusal that lacks the helm's definitely-not-created marker, and the helm sets that marker only for its own
  checkout-conflict, YOLO and fresh-checkout refusals. The supervisor durably records a validation refusal (for example
  a missing session folder) and replays it for the same identity without re-checking, so after the user fixes the cause
  an ordinary retry keeps returning the old error. A page reload, switching to another source's Replace or reopening the
  session view clears it, and nothing says so. The earlier fix for lost Replace retries introduced this, and its
  completion criterion said a deliberate new Replace after an acknowledged result gets a new identity.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user chose "Mark settled refusals as not created". Planned fix: the supervisor tells the
  helm when a keyed create was refused and recorded as failed before anything started, and the helm adds the
  definitely-not-created marker so the UI drops the identity; partial successes and unclear outcomes keep it. Complexity
  gate: a reply field (or equivalent signal) across supervisor, helm and UI plus the UI's existing marker handling; the
  supervisor's durable replay of keyed creates stays as it is. If the fix needs to change that replay or how identities
  are stored, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: after a Replace refused before creating anything, fixing the cause and pressing Replace again
  starts a fresh attempt from both the sidebar and the header; a partial success or unclear outcome still reuses its
  identity. A regression removes the session folder, sees the refusal, restores the folder, retries and observes one
  replacement; run it through the recorder. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `lzwkqynymvkzkuzmxlnvwzuuusrztpkk`; bookmark `plan/replace-retry-identity/02-refusal-recovery`;
  draft PR [#2206](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2206/changes).

## replace-retry-key-splits-across-controls.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main; no runtime reproduction. Replace can be started from the sidebar row or
  from the session header (and the interrupted-session card), and each keeps its own unresolved request identity. If the
  first Replace created the replacement but could not remove the original (a "created the replacement but could not
  remove the original" refusal keeps the identity, as does a lost reply), retrying from the other control sends a new
  identity and the supervisor starts a second replacement agent in the same folder. That breaks SPEC.md's rule that one
  intended create yields one session or a clear error, never two silently, and leaves a gap in the earlier fix
  (`plain-replace-loses-retry-identity.md`). The header's identity also lives in a per-session view, so navigating away
  and back likely loses it.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user chose "Share retry identity per source", adding: "This is also a spec change. If
  multiple buttons exist to do _exactly the same thing_, they should be treated the same except as absolutely required
  at the GUI level." Principle for the spec: controls that perform exactly the same operation on the same target behave
  identically and share that operation's state, such as an unresolved retry identity or a pending confirmation, and
  differ only where the GUI strictly requires it. Planned fix: hold the unresolved Replace identity in page-level state
  keyed by the source session, used by the sidebar, the header and the interrupted card, with one rule for when it is
  dropped. This knowingly goes past the earlier fix's gate of keeping the key in each control's existing state.
  Complexity gate: UI only, in the session list, session view and the page-level state they already share. No helm or
  supervisor change. If it needs either, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md states the same-operation principle; a regression commits the first replacement, fails
  its deletion, retries through the other control and observes exactly one replacement, in both directions; run it
  through the recorder on Chromium and WebKit. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `zqswvnzwyolkxutmskxpkukztownsplz`; bookmark `plan/replace-retry-identity/01-shared-identity`; draft
  PR [#2205](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2205/changes).

## trash-listing-exceeds-control-frame.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed mechanism, much narrower than presented. Each host sends its whole archive listing in one reply,
  an oversized reply (over 8 MiB) is replaced by an error, and the trash dialog needs the full listing to offer any
  delete, so such a host could be neither listed nor cleaned from Farhelm. The app already disables bulk and
  single-entry delete above 10,000 archives (the batch limit SPEC_impl.md accepts), and an ordinary entry is about 300
  bytes, so the reply limit is reached below that count only when average archive paths are many hundreds of bytes long.
  Nobody built such a trash to observe it. No data is lost.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user chose "Declare the scale out of scope". Principle for the spec: the trash is built
  for archive collections well below the 10,000-archive cleanup limit with ordinary path lengths; a host beyond that
  scale may be unlistable in the app, and supporting it is not a goal.
- Completion criteria: the trash section of SPEC.md or SPEC_impl.md states that intended scale and that a host beyond it
  may be unlistable. No code change. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `kxsmypqulzmonvrousnkuxylykxtmywt`, bookmark `plan/triage-spec-rules-oct16/03-trash-scale`; draft PR
  [#2196](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2196/changes).

## trash-body-lacks-keyboard-scroll-focus.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed structurally on current main; the WebKit behavior was not reproduced. The trash dialog's list is
  its own scroller with no tab stop, its buttons go disabled while hosts are unreachable, listings failed, the
  reachability refresh failed, or an operation runs, and Close sits outside it in the header. When the list is taller
  than the dialog in those states, a keyboard-only user of the desktop app or Safari has nothing inside it to focus and
  cannot scroll to the content below the fold; WebKit does not make such scrollers keyboard-focusable (WebKit bug
  277290). The dialog layout filter in FILTER.md does not apply, since it excludes content a keyboard-only user cannot
  reach. The UI has no keyboard-focusable scroll area yet, so this sets the pattern.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user chose "Same remedy as host plans". On the host plan finding, left undecided, they
  noted that keyboard-reachable scrolling should be standard in every GUI component. Planned fix: give the trash list a
  tab stop (`tabindex="0"`), a region role and an accessible name, with a visible focus style. Complexity gate: the
  trash list's markup and its focus style. If the host plan finding is decided first as a general rule, follow that
  decision; otherwise do not widen this change to other dialogs.
- Completion criteria: with every action in the trash list disabled and the list overflowing, a keyboard-only user can
  Tab into the list and scroll it. A WebKit browser regression does exactly that; run it through the recorder on
  Chromium and WebKit. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `pzqxkvmnxkkxwvonwwwnsvmlmxuukxzq`, bookmark
  `plan/keyboard-scroll-regions/02-trash-list`, https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2191/changes.

## host-plans-cannot-receive-keyboard-scroll-focus.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed structurally on current main; the WebKit behavior was not reproduced in the shipped app. Setting
  up or uninstalling Farhelm on a host shows the helm's full plan in a dialog whose header and footer are pinned and
  whose plan area alone scrolls. That area has no tab stop and nothing focusable inside it, the dialog clips its
  overflow, and focus starts on a footer button. When the plan is taller than the space left (a short window, enlarged
  text, long paths), a keyboard-only user of the desktop app or Safari cannot scroll it, because WebKit does not make
  such scrollers keyboard-focusable (WebKit bug 277290); Chromium and Firefox do. SPEC_impl.md requires the full
  concrete action list to be shown before touching the host, but neither spec mentions keyboard access, and the UI has
  no keyboard-focusable scroll area yet. The dialog layout filter in FILTER.md does not apply, since it excludes content
  a keyboard-only user cannot reach.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user, having first left this for later with the comment "This also seems like a SPEC
  thing. We should just have this always be the case as standard in all GUI components.", clarified: "for the host plans
  finding, i meant to close that out but then ALSO make it a spec change". Principle for the spec: every scrollable
  region in the GUI can be reached and scrolled with the keyboard alone, in every engine Farhelm ships on (WebKit
  included); a region whose content holds nothing focusable gets its own tab stop with an accessible name. Planned fix:
  give the plan area of the host setup and uninstall dialogs a tab stop (`tabindex="0"`), a region role and an
  accessible name, with a visible focus style, sharing the pattern with `trash-body-lacks-keyboard-scroll-focus.md`.
  Complexity gate: the spec rule, and the plan areas' markup and focus style. Other scroll regions that break the new
  rule are listed in the PR and reported back as follow-ups, not fixed in this change. If the fix needs more than those
  attributes and a style, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md (or SPEC_impl.md, wherever the GUI's keyboard rules live) states the principle; with an
  overflowing plan, a keyboard-only user can Tab into the plan area and scroll it in both the setup and uninstall
  dialogs. A WebKit browser regression does exactly that; run it through the recorder on Chromium and WebKit. Remove the
  feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `yvoouqnznnslxtptuxswkllxxnzwwqwl`, bookmark
  `plan/keyboard-scroll-regions/01-host-plans`, https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2190/changes.

## claude-trust-cleanup-delays-desktop-start.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main; no runtime reproduction. With the opt-in Claude trust setting on,
  deleting a session removes its managed checkout's trust entry from Claude's settings file in a background step after
  Delete replies. If that step fails (Claude's lock held for its whole 12-second budget) or never runs (the supervisor
  stopped first), a record stays behind, and the only retry is the next supervisor start, before it serves. Startup
  retries each eligible record serially with the full 12-second lock budget, in each of its two pre-serving passes, so
  two records behind a held lock spend about 48 seconds, past the desktop app's 35-second wait for its supervisor, and
  the app reports a startup failure. A lock left behind by a crashed Claude would repeat this on every start (whether
  Claude 2.1.300 leaves its lock behind on a crash is unverified). For retired records the session row was deleted in
  the same transaction that retired the checkout, so the session and its notifications no longer exist; notifications
  about a host or the whole app are a v1 non-goal. A trust entry that is never removed names a folder that no longer
  exists, and startup already refuses to remove it once another checkout reuses that path.
- Decision: on 2026-10-16 the user first asked why startup does this cleanup at all, proposed "just not waiting at all
  on start-up", and then asked for a per-session notification when the lock is held. After the session confirmed that
  the session behind such a record has already been deleted, so there is nowhere to show a notification, the user
  decided: "yeah best efort, no notification, skip immediately w/o wait". Planned fix: at supervisor startup, each
  pending trust removal makes one attempt that does not wait for Claude's lock; if the lock is held, it keeps the record
  for the next start and logs it, with no user-facing notice. The ordinary post-Delete background removal keeps its
  current budget. Complexity gate: the startup call path and a zero-wait (or try-once) use of the existing lock attempt;
  the path-reuse and ownership checks stay as they are. If the fix needs to move cleanup after serving or change the
  record format, stop and return the item to the maintainer.
- Completion criteria: with Claude's lock held and several pending trust records, supervisor startup adds no lock wait,
  the records remain for a later start, and a later start with the lock free removes them. A regression holds the lock,
  starts the supervisor and checks both; run it through the recorder. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `tnwnrnxxtwwszuxuuwtmlvztvwtttwuk`, bookmark `plan/claude-trust-startup-no-wait/01-no-wait`; draft
  PR [#2201](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2201/changes).

## approval-cards-can-obscure-file-disclosure.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (63439c2f); nothing was rendered or run. Before a file link's download
  or Ctrl/⌘-click open, the UI checks only that the hover disclosure is shown, has size, does not overflow and sits
  inside the window (`disclosureFits` in `crates/farhelm-ui/assets/terminal-files.js`); it does not check whether
  anything covers it. The disclosure is drawn at layer 40 and approval cards at layer 45 (`app.css`), and no ancestor of
  the terminal creates a stacking context that reverses that. Cards are centered over the terminal and leave text on
  either side usable, while the disclosure opens to the right of and below the pointer, so a link just left of a card
  can be clicked while the card hides the end of the file name, the deeper directories, or the whole disclosure. The
  consequence is a copy of some other file the session's account can read (up to 100 MB) landing in the user's own
  download folder; native opening stays limited to `.md` and `.txt`, so a covered disclosure cannot make a dangerous
  file type open. Unverified: actual rendering and event delivery in WebKit and the desktop webview. The reviewer also
  noted an adjacent gap outside this finding: web-link hovers share layer 40 and can be covered the same way, and
  web-link clicks have no fits-in-window check at all.
- Decision: on 2026-10-17 the user picked "Refuse when covered, and say so in the spec", with no comment. Principle for
  the spec: a file link's hover counts as disclosing its target only when it is fully visible, inside the window and not
  covered by another Farhelm surface such as an approval card; a click (or modifier-click) whose disclosure is covered
  is refused with the existing refusal explanation, which must itself be visible above the covering surface. Scope: file
  links only; the web-link hover gap was raised with the user and is undecided, so it is not part of this outcome.
  Complexity gate: an intersection test between the disclosure and the visible approval cards in the existing admission
  check, plus layering the refusal message above the cards. If the fix needs general occlusion detection, relayering the
  disclosure above the cards, or changes outside the file-link path, stop and return the item to the maintainer. Revised
  the same day, superseding the file-links-only scope: when asked about the adjacent web-link gap, the user answered
  "same fix for web links". Web-link hovers get the same admission rule: a web-link click is admitted only while its
  hover (with any destination-mismatch warning) is fully visible, inside the window and not covered by an approval card,
  and is otherwise refused with a visible explanation. Web-link clicks have no fits-in-window check today, so the
  web-link part adds that check as well as the covered check. The complexity gate extends to the web-link admission path
  in the same shape; anything beyond that still returns the item to the maintainer. While planning it, the user chose
  that every web-link open is covered, Cmd-click tunnel opens included, accepting that a web link whose hover a small
  window cuts off now refuses; and, once shown that plain URLs printed as text have no hover by design, that the rule
  covers web links that show a hover (program-emitted hyperlinks, and plain URLs only when they show the tunnel hint),
  with plain URLs without a hover opening as before.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md states the principle for both file-link and web-link hovers, beside the existing rule
  that the file disclosure must fit in the window and the rule that the web-link hover is the safeguard against a
  mismatched label. With an approval card shown and a file link whose disclosure overlaps the card, a click and a
  modifier-click are refused with a visible explanation and no transfer starts, while a link whose disclosure is fully
  visible still downloads. A web link whose hover overlaps an approval card or does not fit in the window is refused
  with a visible explanation and opens nothing, while one whose hover is fully visible still opens. Browser regressions
  cover these cases; run them through the recorder on Chromium and WebKit. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `krlyyrymtxlyvrwvrznvottsvmmzlvrr`, bookmark `plan/covered-link-hover-refusal/01-covered-hover`, PR
  <https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2254/changes>.

## file-disclosure-trailing-space-distinction-unverified.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (63439c2f), but harmless; nothing was rendered. The file-link hover
  escapes control characters, Unicode format characters and the shared known-bad list, and preserves repeated spaces,
  but leaves ordinary and other Unicode spaces as they are, and its `pre-wrap` styling lets a trailing space hang
  invisibly. An OSC file target `report.txt%20` therefore shows the same name as `report.txt`, and the directory and
  size lines can match. The trailing space only makes a file less openable: its extension no longer matches `.txt`, so
  the desktop app drops the open hint and refuses to open it. The party that could exploit this is a program on the
  session's host running as the user, which can already write anything into `report.txt` itself; the only constructed
  gain is a decoy beside another account's file in a shared directory such as `/tmp`. SPEC.md's escaping rules do not
  promise that distinct names always look distinct; the "never look alike" rule covers identity labels and excludes
  terminal output. The phrase "so distinct paths never look alike" appears only in the completion criteria of
  `file-disclosure-misses-invisible-path-characters.md` above, whose execution line did not say `complete` although
  #2095 had landed (corrected alongside this entry). Unverified: actual rendering, and whether browsers strip the
  trailing space from the saved name.
- Decision: on 2026-10-17 the user picked "State the limit in SPEC.md", with no comment. Principle for the spec: the
  file-link disclosure escapes unsafe and invisible characters and preserves repeated spaces, but does not guarantee
  that names differing only by leading or trailing spaces, other Unicode spaces, or lookalike letters render
  differently. No code change.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md states that limit beside the file-link disclosure's escaping rules. Remove the feedback
  file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `lytuzvwpulzxolxvokrvvoqznktpxntq`, bookmark `triage/fix-spec-highest-2026-10-17`, combined at the
  user's request with the other two `fix spec` outcomes of this triage; draft PR
  [#2250](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2250/changes).

## pending-menu-arrows-can-ignore-independent-focus.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: mostly already fixed on current main (63439c2f) by #2232 ("honor menu focus during arrow bursts", plan
  `menu-focus-source`): when an item gains focus by pointer or screen reader, the session menu clears its remembered
  arrow request and cancels unsent moves, so the next arrow steps from actual focus. The finding's second case (Home on
  the already-focused first item leaving a request outstanding) is harmless now, because that request names the item
  that has focus. What remains is desktop-only: a focus move already sent across the webview cannot be recalled, so
  within a few milliseconds it can pull focus back to its own target, and the next arrow steps from there. Enter and
  Space activate only the visibly focused button, so nothing runs without the user activating it. This residual was
  accepted in the `menu-arrows-follow-focus` decision "(1)" and again under the `menu-focus-source` complexity gate, and
  is described in its changelog fragment, report and code comments, but not in SPEC.md or SPEC_impl.md. The entry for
  `menu-request-overrides-independent-focus.md` above still states the broader completion criteria. Unverified: the
  desktop timing was not exercised.
- Decision: on 2026-10-17 the user asked for a general spec rule: "if there are tight timing races that occurr whent he
  user simultaneously navigates controls (menu items, switching buttons) within tens of milliseconds of each other,
  unintended behavior on race conditions are acceptable but if it's reasonably simple to fix we should fix it", and to
  fix this item in code too if that is really easy. The session answered that the remaining fix is the focus-source
  design the `menu-focus-source` complexity gate ruled out, so it is not easy, and proposed bounding the rule; the user
  agreed. Principle for the spec: when the user moves between controls (menu items, buttons, switches) by different
  means within tens of milliseconds, a race may leave focus or selection somewhere unexpected, and that is accepted,
  though a reasonably simple fix should still be made; such a race must never run a command or apply a destructive
  action that the user did not activate on a visibly focused control. No code change for this item.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md (or SPEC_impl.md, wherever the GUI's general interaction rules live) states the
  principle, bound included, so the row menu's desktop residual is covered by it. Remove the feedback file and its index
  entry.
- Execution: change `lytuzvwpulzxolxvokrvvoqznktpxntq`, bookmark `triage/fix-spec-highest-2026-10-17`, combined at the
  user's request with the other two `fix spec` outcomes of this triage; draft PR
  [#2250](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2250/changes).

## settled-refusal-proof-can-follow-incomplete-cleanup.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: the code premises are confirmed by reading current main (63439c2f); no fault injection was run. The
  supervisor's proof that a failed create was definitely not accepted requires only a matching request and key lifetime,
  a `Failed` reservation and no session row (`core.rs` around 7387–7406), not confirmed cleanup. Two rollback routes can
  produce it without confirming every process stopped: a tmux creation failure whose rollback sweeps with
  `ScopeKillFailure::Warn`, which accepts a systemd scope kill that could not be confirmed when the portable sweep finds
  nothing; and a failed database confirmation after which a sweep error only enriches the returned error while a
  successful tmux kill still abandons the record. The proof then lets a later plain Replace retire its key and start
  fresh. Both routes need at least two independent rare faults (the first, four rare conditions together), and none
  needs only one. Survivors come from a launch lasting a moment with no prompt; the fresh Replace gets its own session
  and conversation and shares only the folder, and New, Clone or a page reload already allowed starting fresh beside the
  same survivors. The underlying orphaning was triaged in `create-rollback-orphans-unconfirmed-scope.md` and
  `failed-confirmation-discard-session-despite-failed-process.md` and deferred to a Maybe later TODO entry. SPEC.md's
  2026-10-10 two-fault rule accepts a process "keeps running beside a relaunch" on a "remote host", which almost but not
  literally covers a new Replace or the helm machine's own host. SPEC_impl.md says the ordinary rollback paths settle
  "only after confirming nothing is running", and the `abandon_launching_record` docstring repeats it; both are false
  for these routes. In answer to the user's question, the scope case arises only where the launch ran in a systemd
  scope: non-systemd hosts remain supported and get no scope, and "not confirmed" means the scope was still present
  after the kill or `systemctl` failed or errored, for example because the user manager broke after the launch.
  Unverified: what makes the process sweep fail in practice.
- Decision: on 2026-10-17 the user asked what "systemd does not confirm" means and whether non-systemd support was
  dropped; after the answer above they agreed with the recommended spec change. Principle for the spec: the two-fault
  acceptance covers any new launch (Replace, New or Clone as well as a relaunch) on any host, including the helm
  machine's own, and the implementation spec states what rollback actually confirms (that the terminal is gone) rather
  than claiming nothing is running. No behavior change.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md's 2026-10-10 two-fault rule is widened as above; SPEC_impl.md's "only after confirming
  nothing is running" sentence and the `abandon_launching_record` docstring are corrected to match what rollback
  confirms, pointing at the deferred cleanup work. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `lytuzvwpulzxolxvokrvvoqznktpxntq`, bookmark `triage/fix-spec-highest-2026-10-17`, combined at the
  user's request with the other two `fix spec` outcomes of this triage; draft PR
  [#2250](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2250/changes).

## inherited-spawn-carries-workspace-trust.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (1b06488c); nothing was run. The parent's supervisor copies the parent's
  stored launch into a `farhelm spawn --inherit-agent` request unchanged (`handlers.rs` around 3258–3307), the helm
  accepts it with whatever cwd the agent names (`inherited_spawn_resolution`, `agent_requests.rs` around 1712–1778), and
  the step that recomputes workspace trust for the destination explicitly skips inherited spawns (`!inherit_agent`,
  `agent_requests.rs` around 1393–1416), while ordinary create, spawn, managed-checkout create and clone all go through
  it. The supervisor does not re-check trust at create; for Codex it fills the trust marker with the new session's cwd.
  So a Codex, Muse or Pi session launched trusted in a managed checkout (trust switch on, off by default) can spawn into
  an ordinary folder that then loads its own settings, hooks and extensions as if approved, and the trust chains to
  further inherited spawns. The exclusion arrived with #2255 with no recorded reason. By default an approval card
  appears but shows trust only as a raw flag (the plain-language line is `agent-approval-omits-workspace-trust.md`); on
  a host that runs farhelm commands without asking there is no card. SPEC.md "Managed checkouts" says ordinary
  user-selected directories receive no trust override; nothing accepts carrying it into a different folder. Unverified:
  a live run against the vendor CLIs.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user picked the recommended fix: recompute trust for an inherited spawn's destination the
  way clone already does, and say so in the spec.
- Completion criteria: inherited spawns go through the same destination trust normalization as clone (trust dropped
  outside a managed checkout, added inside one when the agent's switch is on) before the approval card and dispatch;
  stored launches whose trust part does not fit the normalization are refused or stripped, with the choice stated in the
  PR; a regression test modeled on `agent_clone_normalizes_trust_for_the_target_before_dispatch`; SPEC.md "Managed
  checkouts" states that an inherited spawn's trust follows its destination. Remove the feedback file and its index
  entry.
- Execution: change `qvnrytqksosxzmvyxqxsvlwzppqmzlsm`, bookmark
  `plan/workspace-trust-destination/01-inherited-spawn-trust`; malformed stored trust segments are refused, preserving
  the source's other command words. Draft PR [#2349](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2349/changes).

## reused-checkout-path-grants-trust.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (1b06488c), not reproduced. Managed-checkout membership for trust
  (`cwd_is_managed`, `working_copies.rs` around 1098–1120) matches allocated records by path ancestry and never calls
  the existing `verify_identity` comparison, and nothing at create re-checks identity before trust is baked into the
  agent's command line. A different folder placed at a recorded checkout's path therefore gets automatic Codex, Muse or
  Pi trust and the managed-checkout mark. Reaching it needs a trust switch on (off by default), a session still
  referencing the checkout, the user removing the folder outside Farhelm and different content appearing at the exact
  path; Farhelm itself never puts other content at a recorded path. It gives an attacker nothing, since anyone able to
  replace the folder can write hooks into the real checkout. SPEC.md's 2026-10-11 acceptance of out-of-band path
  manipulation arguably covers it but names only the archive guard. Unrelated in mechanism to
  `archive-recovery-clears-reused-path-trust.md`.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user picked the identity check before granting trust, "with complexity gate, otherwise
  this is mooted because of spec - users modifying the on-disk etc in ways outside of our direct control is not
  something we add tons of complexity to protect again".
- Completion criteria: the managed-checkout membership read used for trust counts a recorded checkout only when the
  folder at its path still matches the recorded identity; a replaced or missing folder counts as ordinary. A unit test
  replaces an allocated folder at the same path and expects no membership. Complexity gate: if this turns out to need
  more than the small change sketched (reusing the existing identity comparison in that read), stop and record the item
  as covered by SPEC.md's 2026-10-11 out-of-band acceptance instead, with no code change. Either way, remove the
  feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: change `nusnoltoqutlxxqpmxytotkytqunrslm`, bookmark
  `plan/workspace-trust-destination/03-checkout-trust-identity`. The gate held: the membership snapshot reuses the
  existing identity comparison after releasing the database lock, with no new ownership mechanism. Draft PR
  [#2354](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2354/changes).

## unusable-directory-launches-in-home.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code` (the user's pick was `fix code`; their comment asks for the rule in SPEC.md, which makes it
  spec+code).
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (1b06488c) and a private tmux 3.4 experiment; no end-to-end Farhelm
  launch was run. `ensure_cwd_usable` (`core.rs` around 3553–3567) checks only that the path is absolute and a
  directory, and canonicalization also succeeds on a directory that cannot be entered. Create, create retry, Restart,
  Replace and OpenTab pass the folder only as tmux's start directory, and nothing afterwards enforces it: the launch
  spec has no cwd, the launch shim never enters a directory, tabs run a bare login shell, and the scope prefix sets
  none. tmux (pinned 3.7c, `spawn.c`) silently falls back to HOME and then `/` when `chdir` fails; the 3.4 experiment
  showed new-session, new-window and respawn-pane all landing in HOME. Farhelm reports success and keeps showing the
  selected folder, so an agent (possibly with an initial prompt, unattended) acts on HOME. Likely triggers: a recursive
  permission change that strips directories' search bit, a folder owned by someone else, ACLs, network or FUSE mounts
  that answer stat but refuse entry. SPEC.md requires that "a missing or unusable directory still produces a clear
  error"; the earlier `tmux-cwd-format-expanded-*` and `restart-cwd-lossy-non-utf8.md` fixes share the symptom but not
  the trigger. Unverified: macOS privacy protection for Documents and Desktop as a routine trigger.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user picked entering the folder inside the launch and failing clearly otherwise, and
  added: "This should be in SPEC.md. This is NOT an acceptable silent failure. Following a symlink is fine, but this is
  clearly not the intent of the launch and should not fail silently." Principle for the spec: a launch (agent, Restart,
  Replace, terminal tab) either starts in the session's working directory or fails with a clear error naming it; it
  never silently starts somewhere else. Resolving a symlink to its target is not "somewhere else".

## template-wrapper-follows-different-agent.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (1b06488c). An agent request that names a template and also passes a
  different `--agent` keeps the template's wrapper prefix (`apply_template`, `launcher.rs` around 565–590, never clears
  it on an agent change), and the wrapper counts as agent-supplied only when the request's own `--wrapper` set it
  (`agent_launch.rs` around 254–257), so no wrapper card appears. The launcher instead loads the new agent type's
  remembered wrapper. Under default host settings the ordinary approval card still shows the full command, wrapper
  included; only a host that runs farhelm commands without asking but asks before YOLO loses a card entirely. The agent
  cannot inject words: the wrapper is text the user saved. The likely harm is a misconfigured session.
  `plans/reports/agent-wrappers.report.md` flagged the gap without a recorded decision.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user wrote, as a comment naming the outcome: "fix spec: this is as designed. we may later
  choose to support restricting a warpper to agent types but until we do, this is expected behavior. the user picks the
  prefix, and picks the agent type (weather through agent or not). their responsibility to make sure they match."
  Principle for the spec: a wrapper prefix is not tied to an agent type; whoever composes the launch (the user directly
  or through an agent) chooses both, and keeping a template's wrapper when a later edit changes the agent type is
  expected and needs no separate wrapper approval.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md (wrappers or agent-spawned sessions) states the principle, so the command-line behavior
  and the absent wrapper card are covered; no code change. If the report's open decision is still presented as
  unresolved somewhere maintained, point it at this outcome. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `zstnqsvm`, bookmark `plan/agent-spawned-session-rules/01-wrapper-agent-rule`,
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2346/changes. The specification states that a template's wrapper remains
  user-configured when an agent-type flag changes the pairing. The finished agent-wrappers report is retained unchanged
  under the plans editing rules.

  new row to its database (`store.rs` around 6776–6784). Two paths skip that check: a host that reports no installation
  identity, whose new session is kept in memory with no owner check (`manager.rs` around 2034–2118), and a host that

  user chose to fix this half in code and accept the waiting-approval half in the spec. They asked why session IDs are
  not rejected per connection unless they belong to that host; the session's answer was that this fix is exactly that
  rule applied to creates, while the helm can only know which IDs belong to a host from the host itself, so the rule
  cannot cover a host whose remembered sessions were cleared (see `pending-approval-can-cross-host-entries.md`). The
  waiting-approval half is not recorded yet: after that answer the user was offered a cheaper code fix (each card and
  GUI destructive confirmation remembers its host) to weigh against the spec acceptance.

  reply whose session ID a different host owns in the database or holds in memory, whatever happened to the save, with
  the existing conflict error and an immediate refresh of the creating host; the in-memory path also refuses to record
  an ID the database gives to another host. Simulated-host tests cover the no-identity and answer-then-disconnect cases.

## payload-workers-outlive-state-lock.md

- Outcome: `other`.
- Assessment: the lock gap still applies on current main (9ba6b0e9): serving returns and the helm's state-directory lock
  drops without draining blocking payload work (`lib.rs` around 2123–2133), while the payload cache assumes no second
  writer. The trigger is exceptional (realistically a desktop startup failing after the embedded helm is ready, during
  provisioning, plus a second helm claiming the state directory first). A static read lowers the damage claim:
  extraction and the tmux copy write randomly named temp files renamed into place, the cache is per release version, and
  the only byte-mixing writer, the async download, is cancelled at runtime shutdown; the likely worst case is a safe
  failure or a re-download. Not reproduced.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user kept the 2026-10-11 rule (discard rare-trigger findings without shown damage unless
  super cheap) but asked for this one, being close to lasting damage, to be reproduced first.
- Completion criteria: run a focused reproduction in an isolated workspace through the test recorder (scratch-only pause
  hooks, never committed): first confirm a successor can claim the state directory while old extraction work is parked;
  then park an old payload source after staging, after hashing, and after writing its checksum marker, let a new source
  finish, release the old one, and check whether a later lookup counts bytes that differ from the signed archive member
  as a cache hit. Bring the evidence back to the user for a decision; record the result here. The feedback item stays
  until that decision is executed.
- Execution: investigation against main `41e332436529d88d932324dcde0ef08172b0a535`, using scratch-only hooks; recorder
  run `33f2852b-5691-4c8e-a70d-089d4669ecf0`. A real embedded helm returned after readiness while a directly invoked
  signed-fixture extraction stayed parked; a successor acquired its state-directory claim before that worker resumed. A
  new payload source then finished on the same cache. After staging, the old worker failed opening the removed staging
  file for hashing; after hashing and after checksum-marker publication, it failed renaming the removed staging file. At
  all three points, a later independent source reported a network-free cache hit whose bytes matched the signed archive
  member. No incorrect cache hit was observed in these schedules; this is not a proof over every interleaving. The
  source was invoked directly rather than through accepted provisioning, and a full desktop startup failure or runtime
  destruction was not reproduced. Awaiting a new decision; feedback file kept. Change
  `ysxrrvxzlzxxpszrwqxnkxutvmzqnonv`, bookmark `plan/payload-lock-reproduction/01-payload-race-evidence`,
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2356/changes.
- Superseded 2026-10-19: the reproduction's evidence was brought back to the user, who asked how expensive a fix would
  be. Sizing by code reading on main 6d9c1db5 (nothing run) narrowed the trigger: a desktop startup failure after the
  embedded helm is ready cannot have provisioning running (no client exists yet), so the gap opens only when the helm
  panics, or the desktop's embedded shutdown fires, during a host install or update; ordinary Quit, SIGTERM and Ctrl-C
  end the process and leave no gap. Tokio's runtime drop already waits for started blocking work, but the
  state-directory lock drops before it (`lib.rs` around 2025–2133, `token_control.rs` around 79–93). The cheapest sound
  fix found: release the lock only after the runtime is dropped, through synchronous helm entry points that own the lock
  slot outside the runtime, used by the desktop helm thread and `farhelm helm run`. Weaker or costlier alternatives were
  a shared lock copy held by every payload task and making the cache safe for concurrent writers.
- Outcome (2026-10-19, supersedes `other` above): `fix code`.
- Decision (2026-10-19): the user chose fix code, with a size gate instead of a time gate: "the gate shouldn't be in
  time (these time estimates are useless anyway), just have it block if it's more than.... 300 lines".
- Completion criteria: the helm's state-directory lock is released only after every task started on the helm's runtime
  has finished (the runtime has been dropped), on normal return, embedded shutdown and panic unwind, in both the desktop
  embedded helm and `farhelm helm run`; ordinary Quit is unchanged. Do not use a shutdown timeout that would reopen the
  gap. A regression test parks a blocking task on the helm's runtime, triggers shutdown, and shows a second ownership
  attempt is refused while the task is parked and succeeds after it finishes. SPEC_impl.md, "Who owns an accepted
  action", says the helm's state-directory claim outlives all work started on its runtime. Size gate: if the change
  exceeds about 300 lines of diff (code, tests and docs, not counting this ledger, the queue removal and the changelog
  fragment), block and bring it back to the user. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: the helm retains its state-directory claim until its owned runtime finishes teardown, including on panic
  unwind. The CLI and desktop use the same lifetime boundary. A temporary-helm regression parks runtime work, confirms
  that serving ended, verifies a successor is refused, then releases the worker and verifies a new claim succeeds. Token
  rotation can fail during this drain after the control socket closes; ordinary desktop Quit is unchanged. Change
  `vlnrrkollknpuzrkzwlzmpvpvsynrzzn`, bookmark `plan/helm-lock-outlives-work/01-lock-outlives-runtime`,
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2383/changes.

## cancelled-startup-loses-archive-location.md

- Outcome: `fix code` (was `other`; superseded 2026-10-20, see Decision).
- Assessment: still applies on current main (9ba6b0e9). A cancelled supervisor startup leaves archive recovery running
  as blocking work with no ownership (`store.rs` around 3318–3338), and the journal update is guarded only by row state
  (`working_copies.rs` around 1739–1749); in the trash-name collision branch an old worker can point the record at a
  fresh name and then fail its rename, leaving the record naming a nonexistent folder while the files stay in the trash
  unlisted. The trigger stacks a crash mid-Delete, an existing folder at the archive name, a cancelled startup and a
  successor finishing recovery inside a microsecond window that only a stalled filesystem widens. SPEC.md's 2026-10-10
  lifecycle acceptance matches the trigger's shape but rules out "similar lasting damage", so it does not cover this
  wrong durable record. No file loss. Not reproduced.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user kept the 2026-10-11 rule but asked for this one to be reproduced first. Superseded on
  2026-10-20: the reproduction run was stopped after its agent was held up by its model's safety safeguards (reproducing
  meant driving competing supervisors over the state-folder lock and pausing one mid-recovery), and the user chose to
  fix the harm directly without reproducing it, "with a reasonable complexity gate. doesn't have to be super simple but
  it can't explode into thousands of lines of code": guard the journaled trash destination so an attempt working from a
  stale reading is refused before it renames anything. The startup-ownership cause stays out of scope.
- Completion criteria (2026-10-20, superseding the reproduction steps): every write of an already-pending record's
  journaled trash destination succeeds only if the record still holds what the caller last read, so a stale attempt is
  refused and renames nothing; sequential tests show the refusal and that ordinary collision retries still work, with no
  racing supervisors, cancelled startups or pause hooks; within about 200 lines of non-test code and about 500 in total,
  confined to the supervisor's checkout-record code, else block. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: implemented in change `ywmlrrom`, bookmark
  `plan/archive-recovery-reproduction/01-guard-archive-destination`. Initial journaling requires an empty destination;
  pending destination rewrites and rollback compare the previously recorded destination. A changed value refuses the
  write before another rename. Sequential tests cover this refusal and preserve ordinary collision retries. The
  startup-ownership cause remains outside this fix. PR: https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2374/changes.

## pending-approval-can-cross-host-entries.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by reading current main (9ba6b0e9); nothing was run. Session IDs are minted by each host's
  supervisor and the helm keys them fleet-wide (unique index on the bare ID, every per-session route and owner lookup by
  ID alone), with first claim wins and contested IDs refused. Agent Stop, Rename and Restart approvals look up the owner
  before the card and again by ID after approval (`agent_requests.rs` around 346–418, `sessions.rs` around 2536–2538);
  GUI Delete has no host check and plain Replace compares hosts only when "replace with" names one. Removing and
  re-adding a host, or adopting a new identity for it, clears that host's remembered sessions and resets first claim
  wins, so a waiting approval or confirmation shown for host entry A can be sent to a session on entry B; a dishonest
  host can arrange this because it sees every session ID in the fleet. Rejecting foreign IDs per connection cannot close
  it, because the helm learns a host's sessions only from that host. Host entries already carry a helm-assigned,
  never-reused number, and the helm already refuses to connect two entries to one installation identity, but that
  refusal no longer applies once the honest entry is removed.
- Decision: on 2026-10-18 the user first leaned towards accepting this in the spec, then asked whether session IDs and
  other identities could be prefixed by a host UUID so that "the host identity, as determined by the Helm, can never be
  duplicated by a dishonest host" and "any reference to a session is durably associated with that exact host identity".
  After the session explained that the prefix should be a helm-assigned host-entry UUID rather than the supervisor's
  self-reported installation identity, and that this is the redesign it had sized earlier, the user chose it: "costs are
  fine. for the agents/cli, just strat requiring the full id", a UUID rather than the sequential entry number ("a good
  property to have and it doesn't seem to add any real complexity"), and "no small stuf flets just do thew hole redesign
  as part of fix spec+code here", which folds `create-reply-foreign-id-bypasses-cache-refusal.md` into this outcome. For
  an agent naming itself, they chose option (a): the helm accepts a bare ID only when it is the requesting session's own
  ID. They accepted the upgrade costs below. Principle for the spec: a session is identified to the helm, its clients
  and agents by its host entry's helm-assigned UUID together with the supervisor's session ID; nothing a host reports
  can choose or reuse another entry's prefix, and a reference to a session never reaches a different host entry.
- Completion criteria:
  - Every host entry gets a random UUID assigned by the helm, never reused and never taken from anything a host reports.
  - The helm, its REST and event routes, the UI's selection and per-session state, pins, seen state, notification state,
    approval keys and agent commands identify a session by entry UUID plus session ID (one opaque string where that
    keeps call sites simple). A Create, clone or interrupted-create reply can only name a session on the entry that made
    it. Two entries reporting the same bare session ID are two different sessions, so the accepted exception where a
    contested ID blocks access (SPEC.md, session ownership) is removed from the spec.
  - Waiting approval cards and GUI Delete and Replace confirmations act only on the entry they were shown for; a host
    removed and re-added gets a new entry UUID, so stale ones are refused.
  - Agents and the CLI must use the full ID; a bare ID is refused with a pointer to `farhelm agent sessions`, except
    that the helm accepts a bare ID equal to the requesting session's own ID and resolves it on the requesting entry.
  - The helm-to-supervisor protocol keeps bare session IDs; supervisors need no change, so sessions keep running across
    the update and supervisors from older releases keep working and update through the normal path (SPEC.md "Upgrade
    compatibility and client scale").
  - The helm's database migration assigns entry UUIDs and re-keys cached sessions and per-session state using each
    session's cached owner; state for IDs two entries both claim is dropped rather than guessed. Accepted by the user:
    the migration is one-way (no downgrade), contested-ID pins and seen state are lost, and an approval card waiting at
    the moment of the update may get no answer.
  - SPEC.md and SPEC_impl.md state the principle and the rules above; the agent instructions describe full IDs.
  - Remove this feedback file and `create-reply-foreign-id-bypasses-cache-refusal.md`, with their index entries.
- Execution: implemented. Entry-identity foundation in change `ytoksxyppxmkmmvyssxslqnqwtnmwqnz`, bookmark
  `plan/host-entry-session-ids/01-entry-identities`, draft [#2366](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2366/changes).
  Paired viewer state in change `vluozkmkxyzwqkqsymlokuovlpzuvrtu`, bookmark
  `plan/host-entry-session-ids/02-paired-viewer-state`, draft
  [#2367](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2367/changes). Public session references and entry-bound routing in
  change `qnzykzxvyspoxvyrxlrxkkkzlyymklks`, bookmark `plan/host-entry-session-ids/03-public-session-references`, draft
  [#2368](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2368/changes). Entry-local cache and global collision retirement in
  change `umnqtysupwpkwrknytwozuowwmlmlyno`, bookmark `plan/host-entry-session-ids/04-entry-local-cache`, draft
  [#2369](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2369/changes). Both redesign feedback files and index entries are
  removed. Supervisors retain their existing protocol; full references bind routing, viewer state and waiting approvals
  to the selected entry.

  definitely-not-created marker `ActionRefusal::read` (around 2393–2399) reads since #2206. So an unchanged retry after

  then a fresh attempt starts, in every launcher. Principle for the spec: in New, Clone, Replace, Replace with and quick
  launch, a create's retry identity ends only on success or on the helm's definite proof that nothing was created;
  nothing else (an authentication refusal, re-applying an unchanged template) clears it.

## spare-take-adopts-replaced-ready-folder.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main 0154eb35 (not run). Taking a prepared checkout renames the ready folder
  inside `.farhelm-spares` into a claim without checking its recorded identity, and startup's sweep later adopts and
  removes claims that are not live, so a folder someone removed and recreated there can be deleted. The specs conflict:
  SPEC.md's 2026-10-11 ownership paragraph makes out-of-band changes to `.farhelm-spares` unsupported while saying the
  foreign-replacement guard still protects "a folder removed and recreated", SPEC.md's prepared-checkout section says
  replaced directories grant no deletion authority, and SPEC_impl.md says namespace ownership never adopts a replaced
  ready spare while a take never reads the recovery record. Bucket highest as filed.
- Decision: on 2026-10-21 the user said this is just a spec fix and to accept the behavior.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md (and SPEC_impl.md where it promises otherwise) states that anything inside the reserved
  `.farhelm-spares` container that Farhelm did not put there, including a folder removed and recreated, is out of band:
  Farhelm may adopt and delete it, and the foreign-replacement guard does not extend inside that container. Stated as a
  principle covering both this item and `spare-builder-cleans-detected-replacement.md`. No code change. Remove the
  feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; SPEC.md now says the foreign-replacement guard does not extend inside `.farhelm-spares`, so a
  folder in it that Farhelm did not put there, including one removed and recreated, is out of band and may be adopted
  and deleted. SPEC_impl.md says a take moves whatever occupies the ready slot into its claim. No code change; shared
  with `spare-builder-cleans-detected-replacement.md`. jj change `vtrknnxroxsrnovtksyrlxklyrltuzzn`, bookmark
  `plan/triage-specs-oct21/01-spare-container-out-of-band`;
  [draft PR #2563](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2563/changes).

## numeric-token-regex-performance-remains-unresolved.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed on main 0154eb35 by code reading; the slowdown was measured by the reviewer. The numeric-version
  guard in `crates/farhelm-ui/assets/terminal-files.js` lets hyphens be consumed by both its dotted-component class and
  its optional suffix, so a near-match like `1.1` followed by thousands of hyphens and `@` backtracks roughly
  quadratically, bounded by the 8192-unit cap: about 85–125 ms per line in Chromium and WebKit at that length. Nothing
  shows ordinary output looks like that; bucket other on the evidence.
- Decision: on 2026-10-21 the user chose to fix what is super cheap with no real downside and discard the rest. Triage
  judged this super cheap if dropping `-` from the dotted-component class removes the overlap without changing which
  ordinary version tokens the guard accepts.
- Completion criteria: the guard no longer has two ways to consume the same hyphens; existing tests pass and a test
  covers the long near-match staying fast and ordinary version tokens (`1.2-rc.3`, `v1.5x`, `2.0.1+build.5`) staying
  excluded from file links. If the change is not that small, or it changes which ordinary tokens are accepted, discard
  instead (remove the file without a code change). Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `unrvxloxstwxtvwzurmyvwwmnznznonz`, bookmark
  `plan/cheap-ui-hardening-oct21/03-version-guard-backtracking`. Dropping `-` from the dotted-component class alone
  would have changed the accepted tokens (`1.2.3-rc.1+build.5`, `1.0.0-beta+exp.sha.5114f85` and `1.2-` would have
  become file links), so the suffix instead takes three forms that between them accept exactly what the old pattern did.
  Checked against the old pattern on every string of up to eight characters over `1 a . - + _ v` and four million random
  longer ones, with no difference; the long near-match went from about 120 ms to 0.1 ms per call in V8. The separate
  file-name pattern keeps a smaller near-match cost of its own on such a line, outside this outcome. The code, test and
  documentation total 38 added/deleted lines. PR: https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2575/changes.

  save no longer writes the stale whole map over what it re-read; it reapplies only the key change the user made (or an

## agent-stop-kills-shared-personal-tmux.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main 74c80403 (not run). Agents run without `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE`, so a plain
  `tmux` from an agent reaches the user's own server or starts it when none runs; a server started that way sits in the
  launch's scope and carries the session and agent markers, and windows later opened in it from an SSH login are its
  children. Stop and Restart reap the scope and everything the markers claim, so they end the server and the user's
  outside work in it. An ssh ControlMaster the agent starts first has the same shape. SPEC.md covers ending the server
  itself ("Stop and delete reap everything the agent started"; teardown "including background servers") but not the
  user's later work inside it, and never names ssh masters. A code fix cannot tell the agent's own `tmux new -d` jobs
  from the user's windows in the same server.
- Decision: the user chose to accept and document it (2026-10-22 triage page, principle question B), in their words:
  "Yes, this is intentional, and I think at some point we had a discussion, or I had a discussion with some agent, but I
  guess it wasn't specific enough. Yes, this is expected. If you're running a [tmux] from within that Farhelm-managed
  [tmux], you're on your own." Principle: a per-user shared program, such as a personal tmux server or an ssh
  ControlMaster, that a session's agent or tab is the first to start belongs to that session, and ending the session
  (Stop, Restart, Delete, tab close) ends it along with everything later run in it or through it, including work started
  from outside Farhelm.
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md states that principle in "Lifecycle operations" (or "Ownership during cleanup and
  provisioning", next to the background-servers sentence), naming the agent case and ssh masters. The user-documentation
  Doc todo in TODO.md about tab-started services is widened to cover the agent case and ssh masters. No code change.
  Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; draft PR [#2626](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2626/changes) on bookmark
  `plan/triage-docs-oct22/01-shared-program-ownership`, jj change `uqntplyr`.

## tab-owns-first-personal-tmux.md

- Outcome: `fix spec`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main 74c80403 (not run); the item's premise is right. The agent launch
  removes the private server's `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE` only after the login shell's startup files ran, so a
  `[ -z "$TMUX" ]`-guarded tmux autostart never fires there; a tab's shell starts without them, so the guard fires in
  the first tab. On a host with no personal tmux server running, the first tab therefore starts it and owns it, and
  closing the tab (or, with `exec tmux ...`, detaching) ends it with every window in it. The behaviour is accepted in
  SPEC.md "Session view", but its justification ("since the agent's launch has normally already run the same startup
  files, a tab usually finds such a service running and only reuses it", also in SPEC_impl.md and the 2026-09-30 ledger
  reasoning) is false for tmux.
- Decision: the user kept the behaviour and asked for the premise to be corrected (2026-10-22 triage page, principle
  question B; their comment is quoted under `agent-stop-kills-shared-personal-tmux.md`).
- Completion criteria: correct the "usually finds such a service running" sentence in SPEC.md "Session view" and its
  SPEC_impl.md counterpart to say that a tmux autostart guarded by `TMUX` does not fire during the agent's launch, so
  the first tab routinely becomes the owner of the user's tmux server, and that with `exec tmux` a detach ends it.
  Correct the Doc todo in TODO.md that says services started for the agent launch are not affected. No code change.
  Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; draft PR [#2627](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2627/changes) on bookmark
  `plan/triage-docs-oct22/02-tab-tmux-premise`, jj change `yskmnpnp`.

## named-restart-with-keeps-unreported-old-conversation.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed end to end by code reading on main 74c80403 (not run), through the conversation-hooks opt-out
  only. Whether a named Restart with clears the old captured conversation is decided from the harness alone
  (`clear_capture` in `crates/farhelm-supervisor/src/service/core.rs`), before and independently of whether the launch
  is hooked; for Claude and Codex with Farhelm's hooks turned off, no report ever replaces the old capture, so a later
  plain Restart or Resume enters the previous conversation indefinitely. The "reporter unavailable" variant cannot
  happen for Claude or Codex; the Pi and OMP reporter-materialisation failure is decided after the transaction and is a
  different shape. SPEC.md pulls both ways ("A named Restart with keeps the old capture until that report replaces it"
  versus "A launch whose harness cannot report ... has no captured identity").
- Decision: the user chose "Clear the old conversation when hooks are off" (2026-10-22 triage page, accepted
  recommendation).
- Completion criteria: a named Restart with clears the old captured conversation, through the existing Goose
  clear-and-restore path, when Farhelm's conversation hooks are turned off for that harness; a service test covers
  Claude or Codex with hooks off. The Pi and OMP materialisation-failure variant is out of scope; mention it in the PR
  if it stays open. Size gate: about 100 lines as above; over it, block and bring it back. Remove the feedback file and
  its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `vvpnmuwqwxxkztzqmsqzzrmslnyoukws`, bookmark
  `plan/resume-target-fixes-oct22/01-restart-with-hooks-off`. A named Restart with now also clears the old capture,
  through the existing Goose clear-and-restore path, when the hooks opt-out silences the harness reporter

  pre-spawn failure; SPEC.md and SPEC_impl.md say the same. The Pi and OMP reporter-materialisation failure stays open,
  as the outcome scoped. The code, test and documentation total 91 added/deleted lines, below the 100-line gate. PR:
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2636/changes.

  environment, Goose reports have no ownership check, and a report replaces the stored conversation, so a Goose

  sub-agents do so rests on the source research recorded in `lore/2026-09-23-goose-session-tracking.md`, not on a run;

  and OMP, state Pi and Goose child reports as an accepted limitation).
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md "Durability and resume" states that Goose's reporter does not tell a native sub-agent or
  a nested Goose run that inherits it from the foreground conversation, so such a run can replace the session's Resume
  target, and that this is accepted. "First-class harnesses" makes clear this counts among the conversation-tracking
  limits it accepts. No code change. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; draft PR [#2628](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2628/changes) on bookmark
  `plan/triage-docs-oct22/03-goose-child-reports`, jj change `onnkxlnt`.

  that both hosts reach is invisible to them, and the owning host can archive and later permanently delete it. Nothing
  detects a shared checkout root. The reviewer's NFS-home example is probably blocked by the supervisor lock on a shared
  state folder (unverified on NFS); the realistic case is a checkout root on a network mount both hosts see.
- Decision: the user chose to declare it unsupported (2026-10-22 triage page, principle question D: refuse where it is
  cheap; declare the shared checkout folder unsupported).
- Completion criteria: SPEC.md "Maintainer-confirmed decisions" states that a checkout root reachable from more than one
  host is unsupported, and lists it among the unsupported configurations that need no detection. No code change. Remove
  the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: `complete`; draft PR [#2631](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2631/changes) on bookmark
  `plan/triage-docs-oct22/05-shared-checkout-root`, jj change `ukxmrmyo`.

## no-birth-time-checkout-archives-reclone.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main 74c80403 (not run). Allocation stores no creation time when the
  filesystem reports none, and the ownership check then falls back to device and inode alone, which a folder removed and
  re-cloned at the same path can reuse; the archive move, the trash's permanent delete and automatic agent trust all go
  through that check. SPEC.md contradicts itself here: a foreign replacement "must remain untouched" and the guard
  "protects ordinary replacement, such as ... a re-clone", while the device number is used "only where no creation time
  is available". Which supported setups lack creation times is unverified; current ext4, XFS and btrfs installs report
  them.
- Decision: the user chose "No creation time means release, never archive or trust" (2026-10-22 triage page, principle
  question D).
- Completion criteria: a managed checkout recorded without a creation time, whose folder still reports none, counts as
  unconfirmed: Delete releases it with the existing release-without-archiving notice instead of archiving it, the trash
  refuses its permanent delete, and it gets no automatic agent trust. Rows on a filesystem that reports a creation time
  now keep the lenient comparison `inode-reuse-defeats-ownership-check.md` accepted for older rows. SPEC.md "Managed
  checkouts" states this. Size gate: about 100 lines as above; over it, block and bring it back. Remove the feedback
  file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `txsqvnynolqpktxlvvoswqzlszkwvtwv`, bookmark
  `plan/checkout-ownership-oct22/01-no-creation-time-unconfirmed`. Delete releases such a checkout, the trash's
  permanent delete refuses it and a new session started in it is not trusted; legacy rows keep the lenient comparison.
  Restart with in such a folder still trusts as before (follow-up). Size: 108 lines, about the 100-line gate. PR:
  https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2634/changes.

## interrupted-delete-loses-attachments-at-startup.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.

  quarantine before the row is removed; if the supervisor dies in between, or a failed Delete cannot move them back, the
  session survives and the next startup's reconciliation discards the whole quarantine, its attachments included. The
  attachments module's docs promise the opposite. SPEC.md "Partial deletion" leans toward accepting a requested Delete
  removing attachments before failing.

- Completion criteria: startup reconciliation moves a parked attachments directory back when its session still exists
  and that session's attachments directory is absent, keeps rather than discards one it cannot move back, and discards
  only those whose session no longer exists; the attachments module docs and the teardown comment are corrected; a test
  covers a surviving session. Size gate: about 100 lines as above; over it, block and bring it back. Remove the feedback
  file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `wsxzznswkwvoxxrpulluslqxwyqupusw`, bookmark
  `plan/checkout-ownership-oct22/03-restore-surviving-attachments`. Startup moves a parked directory back when its
  session exists and has no attachments directory, keeps it parked when it cannot, and discards it only when the session
  is gone. Size: 117 lines (fix about 40; the rest review-required tests and docs). PR:

## tunnel-can-take-standalone-helm-port.md

- Outcome: `fix spec+code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main 74c80403 (not run). The tunnel's bind (`bind_listener` in
  `crates/farhelm-helm/src/tunnels.rs`) tries the remote port number on `127.0.0.1` first and excludes nothing, so a
  remote service on 7433 gets a tunnel at `127.0.0.1:7433`, the standalone helm's default address, which is free while
  only the desktop app runs. A browser that ever signed in to a standalone helm keeps its device secret in localStorage
  for exactly that origin, so the remote page can read it, and once a standalone helm runs there again the page is
  same-origin with it. SPEC.md "Local authority and trust between hosts": a remote host must not gain access to secrets
  on the helm's machine. Unverified: how often a desktop user still holds a browser credential for 7433.
- Decision: the user chose "Always use a port the operating system picks; never reuse the remote number" (2026-10-22
  triage page, principle question A), after asking why a port another program serves is not already treated as busy
  (answered on the page: 7433 is genuinely free here, and on macOS a wildcard holder may not make the bind fail). This
  reverses the 2026-10-18 same-port preference recorded under `tunnel-port-can-divert-local-traffic.md`.
- Completion criteria: a tunnel always listens on a kernel-chosen port on `127.0.0.1`, never the remote port number,
  bound without address reuse. SPEC.md "Terminal experience" (the tunnel bullet), the tunnel warning in SPEC.md "Local
  authority and trust between hosts" and its UI text, SPEC_impl.md, the user docs and the unreleased changelog fragment
  for the tunnel port warning stop promising or warning about the remote port number; the test pinning the old
  preference is replaced. Covers `tunnel-shadows-busy-wildcard-port.md` too; one change for both is fine. Size gate:
  about 100 lines of diff (code, tests and docs, not counting this ledger, the queue removal or a changelog fragment);
  over it, block and bring it back. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in jj change `wkwutpqqnrvtvunonwysmmlttmzwrpyl`, bookmark
  `plan/tunnel-port-and-link-ranges/02-kernel-chosen-tunnel-port`. Tunnels always listen on a kernel-chosen 127.0.0.1
  port bound without address reuse, never the remote port number; the specs, the tunnel warning, two docs pages and the
  unreleased tunnel-port-warning fragment no longer promise or warn about the remote number. About 127 changed lines of
  code, tests and docs, about 25 of them rewrapped unchanged text, so about 100 lines of real change, within the gate.
  Both tunnel outcomes share this change. [Draft PR #2635](https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2635/changes).

  branch to an ancestor, so the session starts on removed history; a diverged branch fails visibly instead. SPEC.md

  rewind; SPEC.md "Managed checkouts" and SPEC_impl.md say so. Size gate: about 100 lines as above. Remove the feedback

  `plan/checkout-ownership-oct22/05-spare-rewind-clones`. Before moving, the take checks that the prepared commit is an

## cancelled-startup-sweep-outlives-directory-ownership.md

  work that does not hold the state-folder ownership, and a stopped supervisor releases its lock while that work goes

  successor can claim the folder while old work runs; SPEC_impl.md's ownership paragraph covers the supervisor as well
  as the helm; a test shows a successor cannot claim while old blocking work runs. Size gate: about 200 lines (raised

## devbuild-update-strands-host-on-newer-schema.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.
- Assessment: confirmed by code reading on main b97bcfe4 (not run): a devbuild's Update can install a branch whose
  supervisor migrates the host's database forward; the helm's downgrade guard ranks a development-build host as older,
  so a later Update from a release helm installs a supervisor that refuses the newer database and crash-loops, leaving
  the host unreachable from the installed app until the dev build is reinstalled. The helm cannot see a host's
  supervisor database version today. The variant where two branches reuse one migration number and a later supervisor
  misreads the database is unverified.
- Decision: the user rejected refusing at the devbuild end. In their words: "the devbuild behavior is intended, its the
  whole point, its up to me to not install on remote hosts where i also use the release build", and what they want
  instead: "We still allow the devbuil[d]. We're just saying if I accidentally try to then install an 'older' release
  build we'll refuse cleanly rather than bork in undefined ways." (2026-10-22 high-bucket triage page, question 1, with
  the clarification given in conversation.)
- Completion criteria: devbuild's push to remote hosts is unchanged. An Update (from any helm) refuses before changing
  anything, with a message that names the cause and the way out (update from a build at least that new), when the host's
  supervisor database is at a newer schema version than the supervisor it would install. The supervisor reports its
  database schema version to the helm for this; a host whose supervisor does not report one keeps today's behaviour.
  `.agents/devbuild.md` stops presenting the installed app's Update as the way back without that caveat. The same-number
  misread variant is not part of this outcome. Size gate: about 100 lines of diff (code, tests and docs, not counting
  this ledger, the queue removal or a changelog fragment); over it, block and bring it back. Remove the feedback file
  and its index entry.
- Execution: complete in change `uyymnzuvspmxoqlqxutkvomxpxykyrwz`, bookmark
  `plan/update-refuses-newer-host-schema/01-refuse-newer-schema`. The supervisor now reports its database schema version
  in its handshake (`database_schema`, ignored by older peers), and Update refuses before changing anything when that is
  above the schema of the supervisor this helm would install, whether or not the host speaks this helm's protocol
  version; a host that reports none keeps today's behaviour. SPEC.md and `.agents/devbuild.md` say so. The code, test
  and documentation total 329 added/deleted lines. The maintainer accepted the original 288-line fix on 2026-10-23 in
  the plan's Decisions, including the different-protocol case and tests, and waived its size gate. Final review added
  clearer refusal text and compatibility caveats, constructor documentation, and stronger tests within the same design.
  PR: https://github.com/scode/farhelm/pull/2649/changes.

## devbuild-tmux-skips-release-signature.md

- Outcome: `fix code`.

  pushes to remote hosts only against `SHA256SUMS` fetched over TLS, never `SHA256SUMS.minisig`, and reuses the cached

  spec acceptance, and the installer's reason (a fresh machine has no key) does not apply to a checkout carrying the
  release keys.

- Completion criteria: devbuild fetches `SHA256SUMS.minisig` and verifies `SHA256SUMS` against the release key ring
  before trusting the tmux, reusing the helm's existing verifier (for example through a hidden `farhelm` subcommand the
  script calls with the binary it has just built), and refuses on a bad or missing signature; a cached tmux is
  re-checked or re-fetched. The header comment is corrected. Size gate: about 100 lines as above; over it, block and
  bring it back. Remove the feedback file and its index entry.
- Execution: complete: change `onslutqooklvnuwzspznplsprxnqpzvx`, bookmark
  `plan/build-and-tooling-oct22/05-devbuild-tmux-signature`. `scripts/devbuild-mac.sh` now caches the release's
  `SHA256SUMS` and `SHA256SUMS.minisig` with its tmux and on every run verifies them with a new hidden
